title: Leadership & Communication
subtitle: Lead teams, give feedback, run meetings, influence stakeholders, tell stories with data and lead in the AI era
description: A practical course for new and developing leaders, team leads and professionals who need to get things done through others. You will adapt your leadership style, delegate well, motivate and coach people, give and receive feedback, handle difficult conversations and resolve conflict. You will run meetings that produce decisions, write messages that get read, make better group decisions, manage stakeholders, influence without authority and work effectively with your own manager. The course also covers structuring presentations, storytelling with data, confident delivery and Q&A, leading remote and hybrid teams, communicating across cultures and guiding people through change. A new AI-era module shows you how to lead teams that work with AI agents, run async communication across time zones and use AI in everyday management responsibly. Every lesson includes a narrated lecture and hands-on templates, with examples from Pakistan, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK and the US.
outcomes: Adapt leadership style to people and tasks, and delegate with clear authority levels
Give specific, timely feedback with SBI and handle difficult conversations and conflict
Run focused meetings, write BLUF messages and structure better group decisions
Map stakeholders, influence ethically without authority and manage up effectively
Structure persuasive presentations and tell honest, clear stories with data
Lead remote, hybrid and multicultural teams and guide people through change
Lead teams using AI agents, run async communication and use AI in management responsibly

modules.title: Leading teams
modules.summary: Build the foundations of effective leadership: adapting your style, delegating well, and motivating and developing people.

lessons.title: Leadership foundations and adaptive styles
lessons.body:
### Leadership is a set of behaviours, not a title

Leadership is the ability to help a group of people achieve a shared goal. Formal authority helps, but many of the most effective leaders in organisations have no direct reports: project leads, senior specialists, account managers, founders of small teams. What they share is a set of learnable behaviours: setting direction, building trust, enabling people to do their best work and taking responsibility for results.

### Management and leadership

The two overlap, and every team needs both.

| Management focuses on | Leadership focuses on |
|---|---|
| Planning and budgeting | Setting direction and purpose |
| Organising and staffing | Aligning people behind the direction |
| Controlling and problem-solving | Motivating and inspiring |
| Predictability and order | Change and improvement |

A team with management but no leadership runs efficiently in the wrong direction. A team with leadership but no management has energy but misses deadlines.

### Adapting your style

No single style works in every situation. A useful way to think about style is to consider two dimensions: how much **direction** you give (what, how, when) and how much **support** you give (encouragement, listening, involvement in decisions). Situational leadership models suggest matching these to the person's competence and commitment for the specific task.

| Situation | Person's state | Helpful style |
|---|---|---|
| New task, enthusiastic but inexperienced | Low competence, high commitment | **Directing**: clear instructions, close follow-up |
| Learning, some frustration | Some competence, lower commitment | **Coaching**: direction plus encouragement and explanation |
| Capable but unsure | High competence, variable confidence | **Supporting**: listen, encourage, share decisions |
| Expert and motivated | High competence, high commitment | **Delegating**: agree outcomes, step back |

The same person may need directing on one task and delegating on another. A common mistake is to use one style for everyone, usually the style you personally prefer.

### Trust: the foundation

People follow leaders they trust. A practical way to think about trust is that it grows from three things:

1. **Competence:** you know what you are doing, or you know how to find out.
2. **Reliability:** you do what you say, consistently.
3. **Care:** you have people's interests at heart, not only your own.

Trust is built slowly through many small actions and can be lost quickly. Admitting mistakes, giving credit generously and keeping confidences build it; blaming others, overpromising and inconsistency destroy it.

### Setting direction

A team needs to know **where it is going and why it matters**. Create a short, clear statement of purpose and a few priorities:

```
Team purpose: Help small retailers in our region sell online with less effort.
This quarter's priorities:
1. Launch the new onboarding flow (target: 80% of new sellers complete setup in one day)
2. Reduce support response time to under 4 working hours
3. Hire and onboard two engineers
Not a priority this quarter: new marketplace integrations
```

The "not a priority" line is as important as the priorities. It gives people permission to say no.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Amina, a newly promoted team lead at a fictional software company in Lahore, managed five former peers. At first she tried to be "one of the team" and avoided giving direction, then swung to micromanaging when a deadline slipped. With coaching, she adopted a situational approach: close direction for a junior developer on a new payments feature, coaching for a mid-level developer learning to lead code reviews, and delegation for a senior engineer on the architecture. She also wrote a one-page team purpose and priorities. Within two months, the team reported greater clarity, and Amina spent less time firefighting.

### Leadership in different cultural contexts

Expectations of leaders vary. In some workplaces, including many in Pakistan and the Gulf, people may expect leaders to be more directive and to show respect for hierarchy; in others, such as many UK and US workplaces, a more participative style may be expected. Neither is universally better. Effective leaders learn the local norms, explain their approach, and adapt while staying consistent in their values.

### Hands-on: write your team charter and style map

Spend 30 minutes producing two short artefacts you can share with your team this week.

**1. A one-page team charter**

```text
Team purpose (one sentence):  Why do we exist, and for whom?
Top 3 priorities this quarter:  1. ...  2. ...  3. ...
Explicitly NOT a priority:      (things we will say no to or pause)
How we measure success:         2-4 measures we review monthly
How we work together:           response times, meeting rhythm, decision rules
What you can expect from me:    e.g. weekly 1:1s, decisions within 48 hours, credit in public
```

**2. A situational style map** (private, for you)

| Person | Task | Competence (L/M/H) | Commitment (L/M/H) | Style I will use | Next check-in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aisha | Client reporting | H | H | Delegating | Monthly |
| Aisha | Budget forecasting | L | H | Directing | Twice a week |
| Tom | Supplier onboarding | M | L | Coaching | Weekly |

Review the map monthly. The goal is to move each person-task pair towards delegating.

**Optional AI prompt** (anonymise names first):

```text
Act as an experienced leadership coach. Here is my draft team charter: [paste].
1) Point out anything vague or unmeasurable.
2) Suggest what might be missing from "NOT a priority".
3) Ask me three questions a sceptical team member might ask.
Do not rewrite it for me; give feedback I can act on.
```

### Common mistakes

- Using one style for everyone.
- Confusing being liked with being trusted.
- Setting too many priorities, so none are priorities.
- Avoiding decisions to keep everyone happy.
- Doing the team's work instead of leading it.

### Quick self-check

For each person in your team, write down one task they are working on and the style that fits their competence and commitment for that task. Compare it with the style you actually use. Where they differ, plan to adjust this week.

scenes.narration: Picture your first Monday as a team lead. Yesterday you were one of the team. Today, people are looking at you slightly differently, waiting to see what you'll do. Nobody handed you a manual. Here's the good news. Leadership isn't a personality type or a job title. It's a set of behaviours you can learn and practise. In this lecture you'll learn what those behaviours are, how to adapt your style to each person and task, how trust actually gets built, and how to set a clear direction on a single page. By the end, you'll have a team charter you can share this week.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter so much? Because people rarely leave a company only because of the company. Very often, they leave a manager, or they stay because of one. The way you set direction, delegate, give feedback and back people up shapes how they feel every working day. And the stakes have gone up. Teams are more distributed, work changes quickly, and many teams now use AI tools that change who does what. In that world, a leader's job is less about knowing every answer and more about creating clarity, trust and good judgement across the team.

scenes.narration: First, let's separate management from leadership, because every team needs both. Management is about planning, organising, budgeting and solving problems, so that things run predictably. Leadership is about setting direction, aligning people behind it, and motivating them through change. Here's the key idea. A team with management but no leadership runs efficiently in the wrong direction. A team with leadership but no management has energy, but misses deadlines. Most new leaders over-invest in one side, usually the one they're comfortable with. Your aim is to notice which side your team is short of right now.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a good driving instructor. With a nervous beginner on day one, they give clear, step-by-step instructions: mirror, signal, manoeuvre. A few weeks in, they explain why and encourage the learner when they stall. Later, they mostly stay quiet and offer the odd word of confidence. Near the test, they sit back and let the learner drive. Same instructor, four different styles, each matched to where the learner is. That's the core of situational leadership. You adjust how much direction and how much support you give, based on the person's competence and commitment for this particular task.

scenes.narration: So let's make that practical. Picture a grid with two dimensions: direction, meaning what, how and when, and support, meaning listening, encouragement and involving people in decisions. Directing is high direction, lower support, for someone new and keen. Coaching is high on both, for someone learning and a bit frustrated. Supporting is lower direction, high support, for someone capable but unsure. Delegating is low on both, for an expert who's motivated. Notice the phrase for this task. The same person can need directing on budgeting and delegating on client work. The classic mistake is using your favourite style for everyone.

scenes.narration: Now trust. A practical way to think about it is three ingredients: competence, reliability and care. Competence means you know what you're doing, or you know how to find out. Reliability means you do what you say, again and again. Care means people believe you have their interests at heart, not just your own. Trust builds slowly through small actions: following up on promises, giving credit in public, admitting mistakes, keeping confidences. It's lost quickly through the opposite: blaming, taking credit, or saying one thing and doing another. Ask yourself, which of the three ingredients is weakest for me right now?

One of her team, Bilal, is brilliant with angry customers but has never touched the reporting dashboard. Sara realises she's been treating him as an expert on everything. So she splits it. On customer escalations, she delegates fully and just asks for a monthly summary. On reporting, she directs: she sits with him for two sessions, gives a checklist, and reviews his first two reports. Within a month, Bilal is coaching others on escalations and producing reports on his own. Same person, two styles, both appropriate.

The team is busy but scattered: twenty-three active projects, and every stakeholder thinks theirs is top priority. Omar writes a one-page team charter. Purpose: grow repeat online sales profitably. Three priorities for the quarter: the loyalty programme relaunch, the Ramadan campaign, and cutting agency spend by an illustrative fifteen per cent. And, crucially, a list of what's not a priority, including two pet projects. He shares it, invites challenge, and revises it. Six weeks later the active project list is down to eleven, and cycle times are shorter.

scenes.narration: Setting direction is where many leaders stay vague. Values on a poster don't help someone decide what to do on a Tuesday afternoon. What helps is a clear purpose, a small number of priorities, how you'll measure success, and, above all, what you're not going to do. That last part is the hardest and the most useful. It gives people permission to say no. And adapt to your context. In some workplaces in Pakistan, the Gulf or parts of the US, people may expect a more directive leader. In many UK or Scandinavian teams, more consultation is expected. The principle holds, but the delivery changes.

Measures: days to onboard, and errors per month. Then I fill in my style map. Priya on billing: low competence, high commitment, so I'll direct, twice a week. Then I paste an anonymised version into an AI assistant and ask it to find anything vague and three questions a sceptic would ask. It flags that fast isn't defined. I fix it.

Four: a direction statement so vague nobody could disagree with it, which means nobody can use it either. Five: never saying what's not a priority. And six: letting AI write your charter for you. It can critique and question, but the direction has to come from you and your team's real context.

knowledgeCheck.question: A motivated new hire is starting a task they have never done. Which style fits best?
options: Directing: clear instructions and close follow-up
Supporting: listen and let them decide
Delegating: agree the outcome and step back
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Low competence with high commitment calls for clear direction; delegating too early sets them up to struggle.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which action most directly builds trust?
options: Admitting your own mistakes and keeping commitments
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Honesty and reliability build trust; the others erode it.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why include a 'not a priority' line in team priorities?
options: It gives people clarity and permission to say no to other work
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Explicit non-priorities protect focus and give people permission to decline work that does not serve the team's goals; the other options are not the purpose.

lessons.title: Delegating effectively
lessons.body:
### Why delegation matters

Delegation is how leaders multiply their impact and how people grow. Leaders who do not delegate become bottlenecks, burn out and leave their teams underdeveloped. Yet many new managers struggle to delegate, because they can do the work faster themselves, fear losing control, or worry about being seen as lazy.

### What to delegate

Delegate tasks that:

- Others can do well enough now or with some support.
- Would develop someone's skills.
- Recur regularly (so the time invested in teaching pays back).
- Are not the core of your own role (e.g., setting direction, sensitive people issues).

Keep tasks that require your authority or confidentiality, such as performance ratings or sensitive negotiations, unless they are part of a deliberate development plan.

### Levels of delegation

Delegation is not all-or-nothing. Be explicit about the level:

| Level | What you say | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Look into it and report back; I will decide." | Gather supplier options |
| 2 | "Recommend a course of action; I will decide." | Propose a supplier with reasons |
| 3 | "Decide, but tell me before you act." | Select supplier, inform me before signing |
| 4 | "Decide and act; tell me afterwards." | Select and contract supplier within budget |
| 5 | "Decide and act; no need to report back." | Routine purchasing under a threshold |

Confusion about the level causes frustration: you expected a recommendation and got a decision, or they expected authority and got overruled.

### A delegation conversation: step by step

1. **Explain the task and why it matters.** Context helps people make good judgments.
2. **Define the outcome and quality standard.** What does "done" look like?
3. **Agree the level of authority** (from the table).
4. **Clarify resources and constraints:** budget, people, deadlines, policies.
5. **Agree check-in points** proportionate to experience and risk.
6. **Ask them to summarise** the task in their own words.
7. **Follow up as agreed**, and resist taking the task back at the first difficulty.

### Delegation template

```
Task: Prepare the quarterly client satisfaction report
Why it matters: Leadership uses it to decide where to invest in service
Outcome: 4-page report with trends, top 3 issues, recommendations, by 15th
Authority level: 3 – decide content and format; show me before sending
Resources: survey data, last quarter's report, 1 hour with the analytics team
Check-ins: outline review on 5th; draft review on 12th
Development goal: build data storytelling skills
```

### Monkey management

A classic idea in management writing is the "monkey on the back": a problem that someone brings to you and leaves with you ("I'll look into it"). Soon the leader carries everyone's monkeys. Instead, ask: "What do you recommend?" and "What will you do next?" Help them think; do not take the problem.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Khalid, an operations manager at a fictional logistics company in Riyadh, worked late every night reviewing all route plans himself. He delegated route planning for two regions to experienced supervisors at level 4 (decide and act, tell me afterwards) with weekly reviews of on-time performance. For a newer supervisor, he used level 2 (recommend, I decide) for a month before moving to level 3. Khalid regained time for strategic work with major clients, and the supervisors reported feeling more trusted.

### Delegation across cultures and hierarchies

In highly hierarchical settings, team members may hesitate to make decisions even when authorised, or may expect frequent approval. Be explicit and patient: state the authority level clearly, praise good independent decisions, and avoid reversing decisions publicly. In flatter cultures, people may expect more autonomy from the start.

### Hands-on: a delegation brief and tracker

Use this brief for any task you hand over for more than a day. Send it in writing after the conversation so both of you have the same record.

```text
DELEGATION BRIEF
Task:              
Why it matters:    (who uses the result, what decision it feeds)
Done looks like:   (format, quality bar, deadline)
Authority level:   1 look into it | 2 recommend | 3 decide, tell me first | 4 decide, tell me after | 5 own it
Resources:         (budget, people, tools, data access, AI tools approved for this task)
Constraints:       (policies, client rules, confidential data that must not go into AI tools)
Check-ins:         (dates, proportionate to experience and risk)
Development goal:  (what skill this builds)
Summarised back by the delegate: yes / no
```

Keep a simple tracker (a shared sheet or your task tool) so nothing is forgotten:

| Task | Owner | Level | Next check-in | Status | What I will NOT do |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 client survey | Hina | 3 | 12 Sep | Draft in progress | Rewrite her questions |
| Supplier shortlist | Dan | 2 | 9 Sep | Recommendation due | Pick for him |

The last column is deliberate: write down the rescue behaviour you will resist.

**Delegating to people who use AI tools.** State which tools are approved, what data may not be pasted in, and that the delegate remains accountable for checking AI output before it goes anywhere.

### Common mistakes

- Delegating only boring tasks, never developmental ones.
- "Dumping": delegating without context, resources or authority.
- Micromanaging after delegating.
- Taking tasks back when they get difficult.
- Delegating responsibility without authority.
- Forgetting that you remain accountable for the outcome.

### Quick self-check

List everything you did last week. Mark each task: only I can do this; someone could do it now; someone could do it with training. Pick two tasks from the last two categories and delegate them this month using the template.

scenes.narration: Here's a question worth being honest about. How many things on your to-do list right now could someone else on your team do, perhaps not exactly the way you would, but well enough? If the answer is more than two, you've found your biggest leadership opportunity. In this lecture you'll learn what to delegate, how to be explicit about levels of authority, how to run a delegation conversation step by step, and how to stop tasks bouncing back onto your desk. By the end, you'll have a delegation brief you can use tomorrow.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because leaders who don't delegate become bottlenecks. Decisions queue up waiting for them, they work late, and their teams stop growing, because every stretching task stays with the boss. It's also a fairness issue. When you keep the interesting work, you deny people the experience they need to progress. So why do capable managers hold on? Usually three reasons. It's faster to do it myself. I'll lose control. And, quietly, I'll look lazy. Each of those feels true in the short term and is costly in the long term.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a head chef in a busy restaurant. If the head chef insists on cooking every dish personally, the kitchen serves twelve covers a night and everyone else peels potatoes. A great head chef designs the menu, sets the standard, trains each station, and tastes as plates go out. Their impact multiplies through the brigade. Notice what the chef doesn't give away: the menu, the standard and the final check. Delegation isn't abdication. You hand over the task, but you still own the outcome and the standard.

scenes.narration: So what should you delegate? Tasks others can do well enough now, or with some support. Tasks that would develop someone's skills. Tasks that recur, because the time you invest in teaching pays back every month. And tasks that aren't the core of your role. What should you usually keep? Setting direction, performance ratings, sensitive people issues and anything that needs your authority or confidentiality, unless handing it over is a deliberate development step. Here's a quick test. If this task went slightly wrong, could it be fixed? If yes, it's probably delegable.

scenes.narration: Here's the key idea of this lecture. Delegation isn't all or nothing. There are levels, and most frustration comes from not saying which one you mean. Level one: look into it and report back, I'll decide. Level two: recommend a course of action, I'll decide. Level three: decide, but tell me before you act. Level four: decide and act, then tell me. Level five: it's yours, no need to report back. If you expected a recommendation and got a signed contract, or they expected authority and got overruled, the problem wasn't the person. It was the missing level.

scenes.narration: Now the conversation itself, step by step. First, explain the task and why it matters, because context helps people make good judgements. Second, define what done looks like, including quality and deadline. Third, agree the authority level. Fourth, clarify resources and constraints: budget, people, data, and which AI tools are approved. Fifth, agree check-ins proportionate to experience and risk. Sixth, ask them to summarise it back in their own words. That one step catches most misunderstandings. And seventh, follow up as agreed, and resist taking the task back at the first wobble.

She delegates it to Leo, a junior who's organised and keen. She explains why it matters: cash flow depends on it. Done looks like: invoices drafted by the third working day, matching timesheets. Level three: Leo prepares them, Jess approves before they're sent. Two check-ins in month one. Leo summarises it back and spots that two clients need purchase order numbers. By month three, Jess moves him to level four. She's got a day a month back.

Under twenty thousand riyals with an approved supplier, team leads decide at level four and log it. New suppliers: level two, recommend with three quotes. Above the threshold: level three. He also writes down what he won't do: re-open decisions made within the rules. Within a quarter, the approval queue drops to two days.

scenes.narration: Let's talk about the bounce-back. There's a classic idea, sometimes called monkey management. A team member walks in with a problem, the monkey, and walks out without it, because you said, leave it with me, I'll have a think. Now it's on your back. Do that five times a day and you're carrying the whole zoo. Instead, ask: what do you recommend? What options have you considered? Then agree the next step, and who owns it. The monkey stays with them, and you stay available to help, not to rescue.

Resources: last quarter's survey and our survey tool. Constraint: no client names pasted into public AI tools. Check-ins on the fifth and twelfth. scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Delegating only boring tasks, so people never grow. Dumping a task without context, then being disappointed. Leaving the authority level vague. Hovering and micromanaging, or the opposite: disappearing until the deadline. Taking the task back at the first difficulty. Forgetting that you remain accountable, so blaming the person publicly when it goes wrong. And a new one: delegating to someone who'll rely on an AI tool, without saying what data can't go into it or reminding them that they own the checking. Delegate the task, never the judgement about quality.

scenes.narration: How do you know your delegation is working? Look for four signals. First, your calendar: are you spending more of your week on direction, coaching and the few decisions only you can make? Second, cycle time: are decisions and approvals moving faster? Third, growth: are people handling tasks at higher authority levels than three months ago? And fourth, bounce-backs: how many tasks came back to you this month? Keep a simple tally for a few weeks. If the tally isn't falling, look at your own behaviour first. Are you really leaving the monkey where it belongs?

Run the seven-step conversation, including the summary back. Keep the monkey with its owner. And remember you're still accountable for the outcome. lessons.title: Motivating and developing people
lessons.body:
### What motivates people at work

Pay and job security matter: if people feel unfairly paid or insecure, motivation suffers. But beyond a fair baseline, research on motivation (for example self-determination theory) consistently points to three psychological needs:

- **Autonomy:** some control over how, when and with whom work is done.
- **Competence (mastery):** the feeling of growing skills and doing work well.
- **Relatedness (belonging) and purpose:** connection to colleagues and to something that matters.

Leaders cannot "motivate" people directly, but they can create conditions that support these needs.

### Practical levers

| Need | Leader behaviours |
|---|---|
| Autonomy | Agree outcomes, let people choose methods; involve them in decisions; flexible working where possible |
| Mastery | Stretch assignments; feedback; learning time; recognising improvement |
| Purpose | Connect work to customers and impact; share results and stories |
| Belonging | Inclusive meetings; recognition; social connection; fairness |

### One-to-one meetings

Regular one-to-ones are one of the most effective leadership habits. They are the person's meeting, not a status update for you.

```
One-to-one agenda (30 minutes, every 1–2 weeks)
1. Their topics first (10–15 min): what is on your mind?
2. Progress and blockers (5 min): what can I help with?
3. Feedback both ways (5 min)
4. Growth (5 min, at least monthly): skills, career goals, stretch opportunities
5. Agreed actions (2 min)
```

Keep brief notes and follow through on your actions; nothing kills trust faster than forgotten promises.

### Coaching with the GROW model

Coaching helps people find their own solutions, which builds capability and commitment. The **GROW** model is a simple structure:

| Stage | Purpose | Example questions |
|---|---|---|
| **G**oal | What do you want to achieve? | "What would a good outcome look like?" |
| **R**eality | What is happening now? | "What have you tried? What is getting in the way?" |
| **O**ptions | What could you do? | "What are three possible approaches? What else?" |
| **W**ill / Way forward | What will you do? | "Which option will you take? What is your first step, and when?" |

Ask more than you tell. Resist jumping in with the answer, especially when you know it; people remember what they discover.

### Development planning

Most development happens on the job. A widely used rule of thumb suggests learning comes mainly from challenging experiences, then from other people (coaching, feedback, mentoring), and least from formal training. Treat the exact proportions as a heuristic, not a fact, but plan development accordingly:

```
Individual development plan (illustrative)
Goal: Become ready to lead client projects within 12 months
Experiences: Lead the next small client project with support; run two client workshops
People: Monthly mentoring with a senior PM; shadow a client negotiation
Learning: Complete a project management course; read two recommended books
Measures: Client feedback; peer feedback; project delivered on time
Review: Quarterly with manager
```

### Recognition

Recognition is powerful and cheap. Make it **specific** ("Your analysis of the churn data changed our pricing decision"), **timely** and **sincere**. Adapt to preferences: some people enjoy public praise; others prefer a private note. Recognise effort and learning, not only outcomes.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Sara, a marketing manager at a fictional consumer brand in Dubai, noticed her team's energy was low after a restructuring. In one-to-ones she learned that people felt their work was invisible to leadership and that they had no time to learn new skills. She started a monthly "impact share" where team members presented results to senior leaders, protected two hours a week for learning, and gave two people stretch assignments leading campaigns. Engagement survey scores for the team improved the following quarter, and one team member was promoted within the year.

### Hands-on: a one-to-one system and a GROW coaching card

**1. Set up a one-to-one doc for each direct report** (a shared doc or page, newest meeting at the top):

```text
1:1 — [Name] — [Date]
Their topics (first):
Progress / blockers — what can I unblock?
Feedback both ways:
  From me:            (one specific thing, SBI format)
  To me:              "What's one thing I could do differently to help you?"
Growth (monthly):     skill focus, stretch opportunity, learning time booked?
Actions:              [owner] [action] [by when]
```

**2. Keep a GROW card next to you in coaching conversations:**

```text
G  "What would a good outcome look like?"
R  "What's happening now? What have you tried? What's in the way?"
O  "What are three options? What else? What would you advise a friend to do?"
W  "Which option will you take? First step? When? How will I know?"
Rule: I ask at least three questions before I offer any suggestion.
```

**3. A quarterly development plan (one line per person)**

| Person | Career goal | Skill to build | Experience (stretch task) | People (mentor/feedback) | Course/learning | Review date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Using AI to prepare, not to replace you.** You can ask an assistant to suggest coaching questions for a situation or stretch assignments for a skill. Do not paste personal performance details or health information into tools your organisation has not approved, and never let an AI draft recognition that you do not personally mean.

### Common mistakes

- Assuming everyone is motivated by the same things you are.
- Cancelling one-to-ones when busy.
- Giving advice instead of coaching when coaching would build capability.
- Development plans that exist on paper only.
- Generic praise ("great job") that feels hollow.

### Quick self-check

For each team member, can you name their career goal and one thing you have done in the last month to help them towards it? If not, make that the focus of your next one-to-one.

scenes.narration: Think about the best manager you've ever had. Now think about what they actually did. It's rarely a big speech. More often it was small things: they trusted you with something important, they noticed when you'd improved, they had your back in a difficult meeting, and they helped you see where you could go next. In this lecture you'll learn what research suggests motivates people at work, how to run one-to-ones that people value, how to coach with the GROW model, and how to plan development so people actually grow.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because motivated, growing people do better work, stay longer, and help others grow too. And disengagement is expensive. It shows up as quiet quitting, missed ideas and good people leaving. You can't install motivation in someone like software. But you can create the conditions where it's much more likely. And you can do that with habits that take an hour or two a week, not a big programme. That's what we'll build today.

scenes.narration: First, the concept. Pay and security matter a great deal. If people feel unfairly paid or insecure, motivation suffers. But beyond a fair baseline, research on motivation, for example self-determination theory, points to three psychological needs. Autonomy: some control over how, when and with whom I work. Competence, or mastery: the sense that I'm getting better and doing good work. And relatedness: belonging, and a connection to something that matters. Here's the key idea. Your job is to design work and conversations that feed those three needs.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a video game that people can't put down. It gives you choices about how to play: autonomy. It gets steadily harder at just the right pace, and shows you your progress: mastery. And often you play with friends, towards a goal in the story: belonging and purpose. Nobody has to bribe players to keep going. Good work can have the same design. Clear goals, room to choose the route, visible progress, and people you enjoy working with. You're the level designer.

scenes.narration: So how do you do that in practice? The single most effective habit is a regular one-to-one. Thirty minutes every week or two. And here's the rule: it's their meeting, not your status update. Their topics first. Then blockers: what can I unblock for you? Then feedback both ways, including asking, what's one thing I could do differently to help you? Then, at least monthly, growth: skills, career goals and stretch opportunities. Finish with clear actions. And keep brief notes. Nothing destroys trust faster than a promise you forgot.

scenes.narration: Now coaching. When someone brings you a problem, the fastest thing is to tell them the answer. But people remember what they discover, and they build capability. So use GROW. Goal: what would a good outcome look like? Reality: what's happening now, and what have you tried? Options: what are three possible approaches, and what else? Will, or way forward: which will you take, what's the first step, and when? A useful personal rule is to ask at least three questions before you offer a suggestion. It feels slow. It saves enormous time later.

Kamran's instinct is to call the client himself. Instead, he coaches. Goal? A stable scope for the next sprint. Reality? Changes arrive by chat, from three different people. Options? Maria suggests a single change log, one named contact, and a weekly change review. Will? She'll propose it to the client on Thursday. It works, and next time she handles it without asking.

modules.title: Feedback, difficult conversations and conflict
modules.summary: Give and receive feedback that improves performance, handle difficult conversations calmly, and resolve conflict constructively.

lessons.title: Giving feedback that helps
lessons.body:
### Feedback is a gift, if it is usable

Feedback helps people see their impact and improve. But much feedback fails: it is vague ("be more proactive"), too late (in an annual review), or delivered in a way that triggers defensiveness. Effective feedback is **specific, timely, balanced and focused on behaviour, not personality**.

### The SBI model

The **Situation–Behaviour–Impact** model (associated with the Center for Creative Leadership) is a simple structure:

- **Situation:** when and where it happened.
- **Behaviour:** what the person did or said (observable, not interpreted).
- **Impact:** the effect on you, the team, the client or results.

Then add a request or a question.

| Weak feedback | SBI feedback |
|---|---|
| "You are not a team player." | "In this morning's planning meeting (S), you interrupted Omar twice while he was explaining the budget (B). He stopped contributing, and we missed his input on the supplier risk (I). Can we talk about how to make sure everyone is heard?" |
| "Great presentation!" | "In the client pitch yesterday (S), you opened with the client's own sales data and a clear recommendation (B). The client's director said it was the clearest pitch they had seen, and they asked for a proposal (I). Keep doing that." |

### Reinforcing and redirecting feedback

Give both kinds. **Reinforcing** feedback tells people what to keep doing and is often neglected; people need to know what good looks like. **Redirecting** feedback helps people change. Many experienced leaders aim to give considerably more reinforcing than redirecting feedback while ensuring that redirecting feedback is never avoided.

Avoid the "feedback sandwich" (praise–criticism–praise) as a habit: people learn to discount the praise and may miss the message. Be direct and kind instead.

### Timing and setting

- Give feedback **soon** after the event, while details are fresh.
- Give redirecting feedback **privately**; reinforcing feedback can be public if the person is comfortable.
- Check the person's state: if they are upset or rushed, schedule a better time soon.
- Ask permission when appropriate: "Can I share an observation about the client call?"

### A feedback conversation step by step

1. **Open:** "I want to share some feedback about Tuesday's meeting. Is now a good time?"
2. **Deliver SBI:** facts, not judgments.
3. **Pause and ask:** "How did you see it?" Listen; you may be missing context.
4. **Agree the way forward:** "What could you do differently next time?" Add your suggestions if needed.
5. **Close with support:** "I'll help by giving you time to speak first in the next meeting."
6. **Follow up:** notice and reinforce improvement.

### Feedback across cultures

Directness varies widely across cultures and individuals. In some contexts, direct negative feedback in front of others causes serious loss of face; in others, indirect feedback may be missed entirely. In multicultural teams spanning Pakistan, the Gulf, the UK and the US, agree norms openly: "In this team, we give feedback privately, specifically and promptly." Adjust your delivery to the person while keeping the message clear.

### Feedback upward and to peers

Feedback is not only for managers to give. Use SBI with peers and managers too, framed around shared goals: "In the steering meeting (S), when the timeline was presented without the testing phase (B), I think the sponsor left with an unrealistic expectation (I). Would it help if I prepared a slide on testing for next time?"

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Tom, a team lead at a fictional agency in Manchester, had avoided telling a talented designer, Priya, that her missed internal deadlines were delaying client work. When he finally raised it in an annual review, she was upset: "Why didn't you tell me months ago?" Tom changed his approach: weekly check-ins with prompt SBI feedback. When Priya explained she was being pulled into urgent requests from another team, they agreed a process for redirecting such requests through Tom. Deadlines improved within a month.

### Hands-on: SBI feedback builder and a feedback log

**1. Draft every significant piece of feedback with this builder before you deliver it:**

```text
Situation:  When / where, specific    "In Tuesday's client call with Al Noor..."
Behaviour:  Observable, no labels      "...you shared the revised timeline before the client asked."
Impact:     On the work, team, client  "It reassured them; they approved phase two on the call."
Intent:     Reinforce or redirect?     Reinforce
Question:   Invite their view          "What made you decide to raise it early?"
Next step:  (for redirecting only)     "What would you do differently next time?"
```

Check the draft: could a camera have recorded the behaviour? If not, you have written a judgement ("careless", "not a team player") rather than a behaviour. Rewrite it.

**2. Keep a private feedback log** so feedback is balanced, timely and fair across the team:

| Date | Person | Reinforcing / Redirecting | SBI summary | Delivered? | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Review it monthly. If one person has only redirecting entries, or someone has none at all, you have a fairness problem to fix.

**3. Using AI to sharpen, not soften or sharpen too much.** Paste an anonymised draft and ask:

```text
Here is feedback I plan to give, in SBI format: [draft].
Flag any words that are judgements rather than observable behaviour,
anything that could read as harsher or vaguer than I intend,
and suggest one open question to invite their perspective.
Keep my meaning; do not add praise I didn't write.
```

Do not paste names, health details or HR case information into tools your organisation has not approved.

### Common mistakes

- Vague labels ("attitude", "unprofessional").
- Saving feedback for formal reviews.
- Only giving negative feedback.
- Giving feedback when angry.
- Not listening to the other person's view.

### Quick self-check

Think of one behaviour you would like a colleague to continue and one you would like them to change. Write both in SBI format now, then deliver them this week.

scenes.narration: Here's a sentence that makes almost everyone's stomach drop: can I give you some feedback? Why does it feel like a threat, when feedback is how we all improve? Usually because most feedback we've received has been vague, late or about us as people rather than about what we did. In this lecture you'll learn the SBI model, the difference between reinforcing and redirecting feedback, how to time and deliver it, how to adapt it across cultures, and how to give feedback upward and to peers. By the end, you'll have a draft you can deliver this week.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because without feedback, people are guessing. Good performers don't know what to repeat, and struggling performers don't know what to change until it's a formal problem, which is unfair to them. Feedback is also how you shape culture. What you notice and comment on tells the team what really matters, whatever the values poster says. And the cost of avoiding a small piece of feedback today is usually a much harder conversation in three months' time.

scenes.narration: Here's the key idea: feedback should describe what someone did and what effect it had, not who they are. The SBI model, developed at the Center for Creative Leadership, gives you a structure. Situation: when and where, specifically. Behaviour: what the person actually did or said, observable, the kind of thing a camera could record. Impact: the effect it had on you, the team, the client or the work. Then, crucially, invite their view. Situation, behaviour, impact, and a question. That's it.
scenes.onScreen:

• Behaviour: observable actions
• Impact: the effect
• Then ask for their view
scenes.visual: Layout: three connected boxes S, B, I. 0:00 box S fills with a calendar icon; 0:10 box B with a camera icon; 0:20 box I with ripples; 0:35 a fourth speech-bubble box '?' attaches at the end.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think about a sat nav. It doesn't say, you're a bad driver. It says: in two hundred metres, you missed the turning, recalculating route. Situation, behaviour, impact, and a way forward. It's specific, it's neutral, and it's immediate. That's why you trust it and act on it. Now imagine a sat nav that stayed silent for three hours and then said, frankly, your driving this afternoon has been disappointing. Useless. Good feedback works like a good sat nav: timely, specific, and about the route, not the driver.

• Immediate
• Not: 'your driving was disappointing'

scenes.narration: There are two kinds of feedback, and you need both. Reinforcing feedback tells someone what to keep doing. Redirecting feedback tells them what to change. Many leaders only give the second, so every one-to-one feels like a dressing down. Aim to give much more reinforcing than redirecting feedback, and make the reinforcing kind just as specific. Great work is pleasant but tells nobody anything. And a note on the old feedback sandwich, praise, criticism, praise. People learn to wait for the but, and the praise stops meaning anything. Keep them separate and honest.

• Redirect: change
• Much more reinforcing than redirecting
• Skip the 'sandwich'

scenes.narration: Timing and setting matter as much as the words. Give feedback soon, ideally within a day or two, while the details are fresh. Reinforce in public when your culture welcomes it, and redirect in private, always. Choose a moment when the person can actually listen, not two minutes before they present to a client. Check your own state too. If you're angry, wait until you can be curious. And here's the step people skip: after SBI, ask a question. What was your thinking there? You may discover context that changes everything.

• Pick a moment they can listen

• Ask their view

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Nadia manages a small events team in Karachi. Her colleague, Hassan, keeps sending client updates late in the evening, full of typos. Her first instinct is to say, you need to be more professional. Instead she uses SBI. In yesterday's update to the hotel client, which went out at eleven at night, there were three errors in the dates. The client called me this morning worried about the booking. Then she asks: what's going on with timing on those updates? Hassan explains he's covering two roles. Now they fix the real problem: workload.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. At an agency in Riyadh, account director Reem notices that her senior strategist, Yusuf, has pushed back on a client's brief in front of the whole client team for the second time. The client's marketing head later tells Reem she felt embarrassed. Reem books a private conversation. Situation: in Monday's workshop with the client's marketing team. Behaviour: you said their brief was fundamentally wrong, in front of her team. Impact: she told me she felt embarrassed, and she's now asking for a different strategist. Then Reem asks for his view, and they agree how he'll raise disagreement privately first.

scenes.narration: Culture shapes how feedback lands. In some cultures, direct negative feedback is normal and valued. In others, including many workplaces in South Asia, the Gulf and parts of East Asia, it's more often given indirectly, privately and with care for face. Neither is right. What matters is that you're understood and that the person can act. So adjust the wrapping: more context, more private, more softening words where needed, but keep the behaviour and impact specific. Feedback upward and to peers uses the same model. Ask permission first: would it help if I shared an observation about Tuesday's meeting?

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I'm preparing reinforcing feedback for an illustrative analyst, Imran. I open the SBI builder. Situation: Thursday's quarterly review with the finance team. Behaviour: you opened with the one-line answer, then showed only three charts. Impact: the CFO approved the budget change in the meeting, which normally takes two rounds. Then a question: how did you decide what to cut? I paste the anonymised draft into an AI assistant and ask it to flag any judgement words. It flags nothing on this one. Then I log it in my feedback log, and I notice Imran hasn't had redirecting feedback in months. Is that fair to him?

scenes.narration: Measuring success is simple. Does behaviour change? Do people start to ask you for feedback? Is your log balanced across the team and between reinforcing and redirecting? And the hard one: ask for feedback on your feedback. Once a quarter, ask each person, how useful is the feedback you get from me, and how could it be more useful? Notice your reaction when you receive it. If you get defensive, your team will learn that feedback flows only one way. Model receiving well, by saying thank you and asking a follow-up question.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Labels instead of behaviour: you're careless, you're not a team player. Waiting for the annual review. Only redirecting, never reinforcing. The feedback sandwich. Giving feedback in public that should be private. Talking at someone instead of asking their view. Softening so much that the message disappears. And a new one: sending AI-polished feedback by chat to avoid a conversation. Written feedback on something sensitive, without a conversation, almost always lands worse than you intend.

scenes.narration: Let's recap. Feedback describes behaviour and impact, not personality. Use SBI, then ask for their view. Give far more reinforcing than redirecting feedback, and keep them separate. Give it soon, privately when redirecting, adapted to culture but still specific. Your try this now: pick one person, draft one reinforcing piece of feedback using the SBI builder in the lesson, and deliver it within forty-eight hours. Then start your feedback log. keyTakeaways: Effective feedback is specific, timely, balanced and about behaviour, not personality.
Use Situation–Behaviour–Impact, then ask for their view and agree next steps.
Give plenty of reinforcing feedback; never avoid necessary redirecting feedback.
Deliver redirecting feedback privately and adapt style to culture and person.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is the habitual 'feedback sandwich' often ineffective?

lessons.title: Difficult conversations and receiving feedback
lessons.body:
### Why some conversations feel hard

Difficult conversations involve high stakes, differing opinions and strong emotions: underperformance, a rejected promotion, a missed commitment, a disagreement with your manager, or bad news for a client. We tend either to avoid them (silence) or to handle them badly (aggression). Both damage relationships and results.

### Three layers of every difficult conversation

A useful framework from the book *Difficult Conversations* (Stone, Patton and Heen) identifies three conversations happening at once:

1. **The "what happened?" conversation:** disagreements about facts, intentions and blame. Shift from "who is right?" to "how do we each see it?" and from blame to **contribution** (what did each of us contribute to this situation?).
2. **The feelings conversation:** emotions are often the real issue. Acknowledge them rather than ignoring them.
3. **The identity conversation:** what the situation says about us ("Am I competent? Am I a good person?"). Recognising this reduces defensiveness.

### Preparing: step by step

1. **Clarify your purpose:** what outcome do you want for yourself, the other person and the relationship?
2. **Separate facts from stories:** write what you observed versus what you have assumed.
3. **Consider their perspective:** what might they be thinking and feeling? What pressures are they under?
4. **Plan your opening:** a neutral, respectful first sentence that invites dialogue.
5. **Anticipate reactions** and how you will respond calmly.
6. **Choose time and place:** private, unhurried, not immediately before a big meeting.

### Preparation template

```
Purpose: Agree a plan to meet reporting deadlines; keep a good working relationship
Facts: 3 of last 4 weekly reports were 1–2 days late
My story (to test): They do not prioritise reporting
Their possible view: They may be overloaded or lack data on time
Opening: "I'd like to talk about the weekly reports and understand what's making the deadline hard."
Desired outcome: A shared plan with specific changes and a check-in date
```

### During the conversation

- **Open with purpose and curiosity**, not accusation.
- **Share facts, then your interpretation tentatively:** "I noticed X. I'm starting to wonder if Y. How do you see it?"
- **Listen to understand:** paraphrase ("So what you're saying is…"), ask open questions, acknowledge emotions ("I can see this is frustrating").
- **Stay calm:** if emotions rise, slow down; take a break if needed.
- **Move to problem-solving together:** "What could we do differently?"
- **Agree specific next steps** and a follow-up date.

### Receiving feedback well

Receiving feedback is as important a skill as giving it. When feedback stings:

1. **Pause** before responding; notice defensiveness.
2. **Listen fully** and ask clarifying questions: "Can you give me an example?"
3. **Thank the person**; feedback takes courage.
4. **Separate the message from the delivery**; even poorly delivered feedback may contain useful truth.
5. **Reflect and decide** what to act on; you do not have to accept all feedback, but consider it seriously.
6. **Follow up** to show what you changed.

Leaders who visibly seek and act on feedback create cultures where feedback flows freely.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Farah, a finance manager at a fictional company in Karachi, needed to tell a long-serving analyst, Imran, that his reports contained repeated errors. She prepared using the template, opened with curiosity, and learned that Imran was struggling with a new system and was embarrassed to ask for training after many years in the role (an identity concern). Farah acknowledged his experience, arranged system training and paired him with a colleague for two weeks. Error rates dropped, and Imran later said he appreciated how the conversation was handled.

### Delivering bad news

When delivering bad news (e.g., a promotion not granted, a project cancelled):

- Get to the point early; do not bury the message.
- Explain the reasons honestly, within confidentiality limits.
- Acknowledge the impact and allow emotion.
- Focus on what happens next and what support exists.

### Hands-on: a conversation plan you can finish in 20 minutes

```text
DIFFICULT CONVERSATION PLAN
1. Purpose: what outcome do I want for them, for me, for the relationship?
2. The "what happened" story
   My view:                        Their likely view:
   What I don't know yet:
3. Feelings (mine and theirs), named honestly:
4. Identity: what does this conversation threaten for me? for them?
   (e.g. "I'm a fair manager", "I'm good at my job")
5. Opening line (neutral, third-story, under 30 seconds):
   "I'd like to talk about ___. I see it one way and I suspect you see it differently.
    I'd like to understand your view and find a way forward together."
6. Facts I will share (observable, dated):
7. Questions I will ask:
8. My BATNA if we don't agree / what I will do next:
9. Follow-up: note to send, date to check in
```

**Rehearse with AI (optional, anonymised).** Many assistants can role-play a counterpart:

```text
Role-play my colleague in a difficult conversation. Context: [anonymised situation].
They are likely to feel [feelings] and to say [likely responses].
Respond realistically, including some defensiveness. After 6 exchanges, stop and
give me feedback on: whether I listened, whether I blamed, and whether my request was clear.
```

Treat the role-play as rehearsal for your nerves and wording, not a prediction of how the real person will react. For conversations with HR or legal implications (performance improvement, misconduct, health), follow your organisation's policy and involve HR before you start.

### Common mistakes

- Avoiding the conversation until the problem is severe.
- Opening with conclusions ("You are careless").
- Arguing about who is right instead of understanding perspectives.
- Ignoring emotions.
- Ending without clear next steps.

### Quick self-check

Is there a conversation you have been avoiding for more than two weeks? Fill in the preparation template for it now and schedule the conversation.

scenes.narration: Is there a conversation you've been putting off? Perhaps with a colleague who keeps missing deadlines, a manager who took credit for your work, or a client who's become unreasonable. Most of us have at least one. And the longer we wait, the heavier it gets. In this lecture you'll learn why some conversations feel so hard, the three layers underneath every difficult conversation, a step-by-step way to prepare, what to do in the room, and how to deliver bad news with dignity. By the end, you'll have a plan for the conversation you've been avoiding.

scenes.narration: Why do these conversations matter so much? Because avoided conversations don't disappear. They leak. They show up as frustration, gossip, workarounds and eventually good people leaving. And when difficult conversations finally happen late, they tend to happen badly: angry, rushed or by email. Leaders who can have hard conversations early and calmly build teams where problems surface quickly. That's a real performance advantage. It's also a matter of fairness. The person deserves to know there's an issue while they can still do something about it.

• Avoided issues leak
• Late = angry, rushed, email
• Early and calm = problems surface
• Fairness: time to act

scenes.narration: Here's the concept. Research from the Harvard Negotiation Project, in the book Difficult Conversations by Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, suggests every difficult conversation is really three conversations at once. The what happened conversation: who's right, who meant what, who's to blame. The feelings conversation: the emotions sitting under the surface, often unspoken. And the identity conversation: what this says about me. Am I competent? Am I a good person? Here's the key idea. You can't resolve the first layer while the other two are ignored.

• What happened
• Feelings
• Identity
• Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a stone dropped into a still pond. The stone is the event: the missed deadline, the curt email. But what you actually deal with in the conversation are the ripples: hurt, embarrassment, worry about reputation. If you only talk about the stone, you'll keep wondering why the water won't settle. Good difficult conversations acknowledge the ripples. Not with a therapy session, but with a sentence or two. I imagine this has been frustrating for you too. That small acknowledgement often lets the water go calm enough to see the stone clearly.

• The ripples: feelings and identity
• Acknowledge the ripples
• Then the event becomes clear

scenes.narration: So how do you prepare? Step one, purpose. What outcome do you want for them, for you and for the relationship? If the honest answer is to make them feel bad, pause. Step two, map both stories of what happened, including what you don't know. Step three, name the feelings, yours and theirs. Step four, spot the identity threat: what feels at stake for each of you? Step five, write a neutral opening, what the book calls the third story, the version a fair observer would tell. And step six, decide your next step if you don't agree.

scenes.narration: In the room, three moves do most of the work. First, open with your neutral third story, briefly, in under thirty seconds. Something like, I'd like to talk about how handovers have been going. I see it one way and I suspect you see it differently. I'd like to understand your view. Second, listen to learn, not to rebut. Ask, paraphrase, and acknowledge feelings. Third, share your view as your view: the facts you observed, the impact, and what you'd like. Then problem-solve together. If emotions run high, it's fine to pause and come back.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Aaron and Lucy co-run a small bakery in Leeds. Lucy feels Aaron always leaves the early shift to her. Aaron thinks Lucy prefers it. For weeks, tension builds. Lucy prepares. Purpose: a fair rota and no resentment. Feelings: she feels taken for granted. Identity: she's worried that raising it will make her seem petty. She opens with, I'd like to talk about the rota. I think we see it differently, and I'd like to understand how it looks to you. Aaron genuinely hadn't realised. They agree to alternate weeks.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. Sameer leads a product team at a fintech in Islamabad. A senior engineer, Zainab, has missed three sprint commitments, and her code reviews have become short and sharp. Sameer prepares. His story: she's disengaged. Unknowns: what's changed for her? Feelings: he's frustrated, she may be embarrassed. Identity: she's the team's most respected engineer. His opening is neutral. In the conversation, Zainab reveals she's been pulled into a regulatory project by another director and hasn't said no. The real fix is prioritisation, which Sameer escalates. Her next two sprints are on target.

scenes.narration: Delivering bad news is its own skill: redundancy, a rejected promotion, a cancelled project. Say it early in the conversation, clearly, in the first minute. Don't bury it under small talk. Give the reason honestly, as far as you're able. Then stop talking, and let the person react. Acknowledge the impact. Explain what happens next and what support exists. Don't argue with emotions, and don't say, I know how you feel. For anything with HR or legal implications, follow your organisation's policy and involve HR before you start.

lessons.title: Resolving conflict constructively
lessons.body:
### Conflict is normal

Where people care about outcomes, disagreements happen. Conflict about **ideas and tasks** can improve decisions by surfacing options and risks. Conflict about **people and relationships** usually harms performance. Leaders aim to encourage the first and manage the second.

### Conflict styles

The Thomas–Kilmann model describes five styles along two dimensions: assertiveness (concern for your own goals) and cooperativeness (concern for others' goals).

| Style | Assertive | Cooperative | When useful | Risk if overused |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Competing** | High | Low | Emergencies; unpopular but necessary decisions | Damaged relationships |
| **Collaborating** | High | High | Important issues where both sides' needs matter | Time-consuming |
| **Compromising** | Medium | Medium | Moderate stakes; time pressure | Nobody fully satisfied |
| **Avoiding** | Low | Low | Trivial issues; cooling-off needed | Problems grow |
| **Accommodating** | Low | High | Relationship matters more; you are wrong | Resentment; being exploited |

Effective people use all five, choosing deliberately. Most of us have a default; know yours.

### Interests, not positions

A **position** is what someone says they want; an **interest** is why they want it. Conflicts are easier to resolve at the level of interests.

*Illustrative.* Sales wants the product launched in March (position) to hit quarterly targets (interest). Engineering wants June (position) to avoid shipping with known security gaps (interest). Exploring interests reveals options: launch a limited version in March to selected customers with the security-critical features, full launch in June. Both interests are met.

### A mediation process for leaders

When two team members are in conflict:

1. **Meet each separately first:** listen, understand interests and emotions, explain the process.
2. **Bring them together** with ground rules: one speaks at a time, focus on the issue, respect.
3. **Each describes their view**; the other paraphrases it until the first agrees it is accurate.
4. **Identify shared goals and interests.**
5. **Generate options together**; avoid judging too early.
6. **Agree actions**, write them down, set a follow-up.
7. **Follow up** and recognise progress.

### Escalation and when to involve HR

If conflict involves harassment, discrimination, bullying, safety or legal issues, follow your organisation's policies and involve HR or appropriate channels promptly. Mediation by a line manager is not appropriate for such cases.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Two team leads at a fictional hospital in Abu Dhabi, one from nursing and one from facilities, repeatedly clashed over cleaning schedules in a ward. Each saw the other as unreasonable. Their manager met each separately, then together. Nursing's interest was infection control during peak patient hours; facilities' interest was completing work within staff shift patterns without overtime. They agreed a revised schedule with a short, targeted clean during peak hours and a deep clean after the evening medication round. Complaints dropped, and the two leads began meeting monthly to review.

### Healthy disagreement in teams

To encourage productive task conflict:

- Ask for dissent explicitly: "What are we missing? Who sees it differently?"
- Assign a rotating "devil's advocate" for big decisions.
- Separate idea generation from evaluation.
- Once decided, agree to **disagree and commit**: people support the decision even if they argued against it.

### Hands-on: a mediation kit for team leads

**1. Pre-meeting (separately with each person, 20 minutes each):**

```text
"What's happened, from your point of view?"
"What matters most to you in how this gets resolved?"   (interest)
"What would you need from [other person] to work well together?"
"What are you willing to do differently?"
"Is there anything that would make a joint conversation unsafe?"  (if yes, stop and involve HR)
```

**2. Joint meeting agenda (45–60 minutes):**

```text
1. Ground rules (2 min): one speaker at a time; describe behaviour, not character; confidential
2. Each person's view uninterrupted (5 min each); the other paraphrases back
3. Leader summarises shared interests and differences (5 min)
4. Generate options together (15 min): at least 5 before judging
5. Agree specifics (10 min): who does what, by when, how you'll raise issues next time
6. Written summary sent the same day; check-in booked in 2 weeks
```

**3. Working agreement template** (the output of the joint meeting):

| Situation | What we'll do | Owner | Review |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hand-offs between design and development | Hand-off checklist in the ticket before status changes | Both | 2 weeks |
| Disagreement on priority | Raise privately within 24 hours, then escalate together to the lead | Both | 2 weeks |

Stop mediating and escalate to HR if there are allegations of harassment, discrimination, bullying, threats, safety concerns or potential misconduct. Those are not "conflicts" to be mediated by a line manager.

### Common mistakes

- Avoiding conflict until it becomes personal.
- Taking sides before hearing both parties.
- Focusing on positions rather than interests.
- Resolving the immediate issue but not the underlying pattern.
- Treating serious misconduct as a "personality clash".

### Quick self-check

Which conflict style do you use most often? Think of a current disagreement: which style would actually serve the situation best, and what would you do differently to use it?

### Conflict with clients and external partners

The same principles apply outside your organisation, with extra care. With clients, separate the relationship from the issue: acknowledge their frustration, restate the shared goal (a successful project), and move to interests and options. Put agreements in writing, because external disputes can have contractual consequences. If the conflict involves commercial terms, involve your account lead or legal colleagues early rather than improvising concessions under pressure.

### After the conflict

Resolution is not the end. Check in with both parties a week or two later: is the agreement working, and has the relationship recovered? Small follow-ups prevent old tensions from resurfacing and show that you take people's concerns seriously.

scenes.narration: Two of your best people have stopped talking to each other. Meetings are tense. Messages are cc'd to you as evidence. Everyone else is walking on eggshells. Sound familiar? Conflict is part of any team that cares about its work. The question isn't how to avoid it, but how to make it productive. In this lecture, you'll learn the five conflict styles and when each fits, how to move from positions to interests, a simple mediation process for leaders, and when to stop and escalate. By the end, you'll have a mediation kit ready to use.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Unresolved conflict is expensive. It slows decisions, drains energy and, left alone, pushes good people out. But the absence of conflict isn't a good sign either. Teams that never disagree are often suppressing ideas, and they make worse decisions. What you want is healthy conflict about tasks and ideas, and very little conflict about personalities. Your role as a leader is to keep disagreement focused on the work, surface it early, and help people resolve it themselves wherever possible.

scenes.narration: First, the concept of conflict styles. A widely used framework, the Thomas-Kilmann model, describes five styles based on two dimensions: how assertive you are about your own concerns, and how cooperative you are with the other person's. Competing: high assertive, low cooperative. Accommodating: the reverse. Avoiding: low on both. Compromising: middle on both. And collaborating: high on both. Here's the key idea: each style has a place. Competing fits a genuine emergency. Avoiding fits a trivial issue. But for important issues with ongoing relationships, collaborating is usually worth the extra time.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Conflict styles are like the gears in a car. First gear is powerful but noisy, fine for pulling away, terrible on the motorway. Top gear is efficient at speed, useless on a steep hill. A good driver changes gear for the road. Most of us, though, have a favourite gear we use everywhere. Some always compete. Some always avoid. Notice your default gear. Then ask, before each conflict, what does this road actually need?

scenes.narration: Next, positions and interests, which you may know from negotiation. A position is what someone says they want. I need the designer full-time on my project. An interest is why. My launch date is fixed and I'm worried about quality. When two people argue positions, only one can win. When you uncover interests, you often find solutions that satisfy both. So ask: what's important to you about that? What are you worried might happen? Then look for options that meet both sets of interests.

scenes.narration: Now a mediation process you can run as a team lead. Step one: meet each person separately first. Understand their view, their interests and what they'd need. Step two: bring them together with simple ground rules: one speaker at a time, describe behaviour not character. Step three: each person explains their view without interruption, and the other paraphrases it back. Step four: you summarise shared interests and differences. Step five: generate options together, at least five before judging. Step six: agree specifics and put them in writing. Then check in two weeks later.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. In a small agency in Birmingham, the copywriter, Ella, and the designer, Josh, keep clashing over deadlines. Ella says Josh never sends layouts on time. Josh says Ella changes the copy after he's designed around it. Their manager, Priya, meets each of them first, then together. Interests surface: Ella wants time to refine, Josh wants stable copy. They agree a simple rule: copy is locked before design starts, with one agreed revision window. The clashes stop within a fortnight.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. At a hospital supplies distributor in Jeddah, the sales manager, Abdullah, and the warehouse manager, Noura, are in open conflict. Sales promises next-day delivery to win orders; the warehouse misses them and gets blamed. The regional director mediates. In separate meetings she hears the interests: sales needs a competitive promise, the warehouse needs predictable volume. Together they agree options: a same-day cut-off time, a daily volume forecast from sales, and a shared on-time delivery measure owned by both. Within two months, missed deliveries fall and the blame emails stop.

scenes.narration: Now, a crucial boundary. Not every conflict should be mediated by a line manager. If there are allegations of harassment, bullying, discrimination, threats, safety risks or potential misconduct, stop. Those are not disagreements to smooth over. Follow your organisation's policy, document what you've been told, and involve HR or the appropriate function straight away. Mediating them informally can harm the person who raised the concern and expose the organisation. It's also why, in the separate pre-meetings, you ask: is there anything that would make a joint conversation unsafe for you?

In the joint meeting, I set the ground rules and ask each to paraphrase the other. Then options: a shared checklist, a single owner per client, a handover meeting. scenes.narration: How do you know the conflict is resolved, not just quiet? Look at behaviour, not words. Are they communicating directly rather than through you? Are hand-offs working? Have the cc'd evidence emails stopped? Do they both describe the agreement the same way when you ask separately? At the two-week check-in, ask each person, what's working, and what still needs adjusting? And look at yourself. If you're still the go-between, you haven't resolved the conflict. You've just absorbed it.
