modules.title: Meetings, writing and decisions
modules.summary: Run meetings that produce decisions, write messages that get read and acted on, and make better group decisions.

lessons.title: Meetings that work
lessons.body:
### The cost of bad meetings

Meetings are expensive: a one-hour meeting with eight people consumes eight hours of working time, plus preparation and context switching. Yet many meetings have no clear purpose, no agenda and no outcome. Good leaders protect everyone's time by running fewer, better meetings.

### Step 1: should this be a meeting?

Hold a meeting when you need real-time discussion: to decide, solve a problem, build relationships or handle sensitive topics. Use written, asynchronous updates for information sharing.

```
Need                              Better format
Share status updates              Written update or dashboard
Make a decision with trade-offs   Meeting (with pre-read)
Brainstorm options                Workshop or async doc + short meeting
Deliver sensitive news            Meeting (1:1 or small group)
Quick question                    Chat message
```

### Step 2: design the meeting

- **Purpose:** one sentence. "Decide which supplier to shortlist."
- **Outcome:** what will exist at the end? A decision, a list of options, an agreed plan.
- **Participants:** only those needed to decide, contribute expertise or implement. Others receive notes.
- **Agenda:** topics framed as questions, with time allocations and owners.
- **Pre-read:** sent at least a day ahead for decision meetings.

```
Meeting: Supplier shortlist decision (45 min)
Purpose: Decide which 2 suppliers go to final negotiation
Pre-read: Evaluation matrix (attached), sent Monday
Agenda:
1. Clarifying questions on the matrix (10 min) – Procurement lead
2. Discussion: risks and trade-offs (20 min) – All
3. Decision (10 min) – Operations director decides
4. Next steps and owners (5 min) – Chair
```

### Step 3: run the meeting

- Start on time; restate purpose and desired outcome.
- Assign roles: **chair/facilitator**, **timekeeper**, **note-taker**.
- Make space for quieter voices: go round the table, or ask people to write ideas first.
- Keep to the agenda; park unrelated topics in a "parking lot".
- Summarise decisions and actions as you go.

### Step 4: close and follow up

End with clear actions: **who does what by when**. Send notes within 24 hours:

```
Decisions:
- Shortlist: Supplier A and Supplier C (decided by Operations Director)
Actions:
- Negotiate terms with A and C – Procurement lead – by 20 May
- Reference checks – Ops manager – by 15 May
Parking lot: Review of warehouse contract (to next month's agenda)
```

### Recurring meetings

Review recurring meetings every quarter: is each still needed? Could it be shorter or less frequent? Could fewer people attend? Many organisations find that a periodic "meeting audit" frees significant time.

### Hybrid meetings

When some participants are remote:

- Everyone joins from their own device, even people in the same room, if audio allows, so remote participants are not disadvantaged.
- Use a shared document or whiteboard visible to all.
- The facilitator actively invites remote participants to speak.
- Consider time zones: rotate inconvenient times fairly across locations.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* A fictional regional office of an engineering firm in Doha ran a weekly two-hour management meeting with 15 attendees. After an audit, it became a 45-minute decision meeting with 7 people and a pre-read, while status updates moved to a written weekly summary. Managers estimated they recovered several hours each week, and decisions were made faster because pre-reads meant discussion started from shared facts.

### Hands-on: a meeting design card, AI notes policy and a calendar audit

**1. Meeting design card** (paste it into every invite you send):

```text
Purpose:        Decide | Generate ideas | Align | Inform   (circle one)
Outcome:        "By the end we will have ___"
Pre-read:       link, sent 24 hours before; 3 questions to consider
Agenda:         item — owner — minutes — decision or discussion?
Who and why:    each attendee's role (decider, input, informed later)
Decision rule:  who decides, and how (see group-decisions lesson)
Close:          decisions, actions (owner + date), what we tell others
```

**2. A team policy for AI meeting assistants.** Many video platforms (for example Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet, depending on your plan and settings) can transcribe and summarise meetings. Agree the rules once:

```text
- Announce recording/transcription at the start; honour anyone who asks to turn it off.
- No AI notetakers in 1:1s, HR, health, legal or disciplinary conversations.
- A named human checks the AI summary and corrects decisions/owners before it is shared.
- Summaries go to attendees only; follow your data-retention policy.
- The AI summary is not the decision record; the owner's written close is.
```

Recording and transcription are subject to privacy law and workplace policy in your country (for example UK GDPR in the UK). Check with your data protection lead before rolling out notetakers.

**3. A 15-minute calendar audit.** Export or list last fortnight's recurring meetings and score each:

| Meeting | Purpose clear? | Decisions made? | Could it be async? | Keep / shorten / merge / cancel |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Cancel or convert at least one meeting to an async update this month.

### Common mistakes

- No agenda or purpose.
- Inviting everyone "to be safe".
- Using meetings to read slides aloud.
- Letting the loudest voices dominate.
- Ending without clear decisions and owners.

### Quick self-check

Look at your calendar for next week. For each meeting you own, write its purpose in one sentence. Cancel, shorten or convert to written updates any meeting where you cannot.

### Facilitation techniques worth learning

A few simple techniques make a big difference. **Silent brainstorming**: everyone writes ideas for three minutes before discussion, which prevents the first idea from anchoring the group. **Dot voting**: participants place a limited number of votes on options to reveal preferences quickly. **Round-robin**: each person speaks in turn, which is especially useful in hierarchical or multicultural groups. **Timeboxing**: agree a fixed time for each item and stick to it, parking unresolved points. Choose techniques to fit the meeting's purpose.

### Meeting-free time

Many teams protect blocks of focus time, such as a meeting-free morning each week. This supports deep work and signals that meetings are a cost, not a default.

scenes.narration: Think about the last meeting you left wondering why you were there. No clear purpose, the same three people talking, and at the end, nobody quite sure what was decided. Now multiply that by every recurring meeting in your week. Meetings are one of the biggest uses of a team's time, and one of the easiest places to win it back. In this lecture, you'll learn a four-step method: decide whether it should be a meeting at all, design it, run it well, and close it properly. We'll also cover hybrid meetings and AI notetakers.
scenes.onScreen:
Meetings that work
• Should it be a meeting?
• Design
• Run
• Close and follow up
• Hybrid and AI notetakers
scenes.visual: Layout: a crowded weekly calendar grid. 0:00 meeting blocks pile in until the week is solid; 0:15 a timer counts total hours; 0:25 four step chips appear: Question, Design, Run, Close; 0:40 two extra chips for hybrid and AI.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because a one-hour meeting with eight people isn't an hour. It's eight hours of your team's time. Bad meetings also have hidden costs: decisions get delayed, the same topic is revisited again and again, and the quieter people, often with the best ideas, stop contributing. Good meetings do the opposite. They produce decisions and commitments that would take days of messages to reach. The aim isn't fewer meetings for the sake of it. It's that every meeting earns its place.
scenes.onScreen:
Why it matters
• 1 hour × 8 people = 8 hours
• Delayed and revisited decisions
• Quiet voices lost
• Every meeting must earn its place
scenes.visual: Layout: a clock with eight small avatar icons around it. 0:00 the minute hand sweeps once; 0:10 a counter multiplies '1 hour' into '8 hours'; 0:25 a looping arrow labelled 'revisited again'; 0:40 a badge 'earns its place' stamps onto a single meeting block.

scenes.narration: Here's the concept. Every meeting should have one main purpose. Decide. Generate ideas. Align, meaning get people on the same page and surface concerns. Or inform, and inform is the one that should most often be an email, a document or a short recorded video instead. Once you know the purpose, write the outcome in a single sentence: by the end, we will have chosen a supplier, or by the end, we will have three options for the Eid campaign. Here's the key idea. If you can't write that sentence, you're not ready to send the invite.
scenes.onScreen:
One purpose per meeting
• Decide
• Generate ideas
• Align
• Inform (often async)
• Write the outcome sentence first
scenes.visual: Layout: four purpose cards laid out in a row. 0:00 cards flip one by one; 0:20 the 'Inform' card slides into an envelope labelled 'async'; 0:35 an outcome sentence types beneath: 'By the end we will have...'; 0:45 an invite button stays greyed until the sentence completes.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. A good meeting is like a well-run flight. Before take-off, there's a flight plan: destination, route, fuel. During the flight, the pilot keeps to the route, handles turbulence, and doesn't take detours because someone fancies a look at the mountains. At landing, there's a clear arrival and everyone knows where to collect their bags. Many meetings take off without a destination, circle for an hour, and land somewhere nobody expected. Your job is to be the pilot: plan, fly the route, and land deliberately.
scenes.onScreen:
The flight
• Flight plan: purpose, agenda, pre-read
• In flight: stay on route
• Landing: decisions and actions
• Don't circle
scenes.visual: Layout: a flight map. 0:00 a dotted route from 'Purpose' to 'Outcome'; 0:12 a plane follows it smoothly; 0:25 a second plane circles aimlessly with a 'no destination' tag; 0:40 the first plane lands with a baggage-carousel icon labelled 'actions'.

scenes.narration: Step two, design. Build an agenda with owners and timings, and for each item say whether it's a decision or a discussion. Invite only the people you need, and be clear about each person's role: decider, input, or informed afterwards. Send a short pre-read at least a day before, with two or three questions to consider. Then use the first few minutes of the meeting for silent reading if people haven't read it. Some companies famously start meetings with a silent read of a written memo. It levels the playing field and speeds up everything that follows.
scenes.onScreen:
Design
• Agenda: owner, minutes, decision or discussion
• Invite by role
• Pre-read 24 hours ahead
• Optional silent read at the start
scenes.visual: Layout: an agenda table builds row by row with columns 'item', 'owner', 'minutes', 'type'. 0:25 an attendee list sorts itself into decider, input, informed; 0:40 a document icon with a clock '24h before'; 0:50 a room icon with 'silent reading 5 min'.

scenes.narration: Step three, run it. Start on time, restate the purpose and outcome, and name the decision rule. Keep to the agenda and park off-topic items visibly in a parking lot. Draw in quieter voices deliberately, for example with a quick round or by asking people to write ideas first. In hybrid meetings, fairness takes extra effort. If one person is remote, everyone joins from their own screen, and the chair checks the chat and the remote faces first. Step four, close. Summarise decisions, owners, deadlines and what you'll tell others. Then send it in writing within a day.
scenes.onScreen:
Run and close
• Start on time, restate outcome
• Parking lot
• Draw in quiet voices
• Hybrid: remote first
• Close: decisions, owners, dates, comms
scenes.visual: Layout: split screen. 0:00 left side shows a meeting room with a parking-lot board collecting sticky notes; 0:20 a round-robin arrow circles the table; 0:30 right side shows a hybrid grid with remote tiles highlighted first; 0:45 a summary card slides out with four ticked fields.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Tariq runs a small property agency in Lahore. His Monday team meeting has drifted to ninety minutes of updates. He changes it. Updates go into a shared document by Sunday evening. The meeting shrinks to thirty minutes with only two items: blockers, and one decision for the week. On the first week, the decision is whether to pause a slow-moving listing campaign. They decide in ten minutes, because everyone read the numbers beforehand. The team gets an hour back every week.

Worked example 1: Tariq in Lahore (illustrative)
• 90 minutes of updates
• Updates move to a shared doc
• 30 minutes: blockers + one decision
• One hour back weekly

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. Hannah is chief of staff at a fifty-person software firm in Austin. The leadership team meets for two hours every Tuesday, yet decisions keep slipping. She runs a calendar audit and finds that most agenda items are updates. She redesigns the meeting: a written pre-read due Monday, silent reading for the first ten minutes, and only items marked decide or align on the agenda. Each decision gets an owner and a date in the close. Within a quarter, the meeting is down to seventy-five minutes and the backlog of open decisions has roughly halved.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 2: Hannah in Austin (illustrative)
• 2-hour weekly meeting, slipping decisions
• Audit: mostly updates
• Pre-read + silent read + decide/align only
• 75 minutes; open decisions roughly halved

scenes.narration: Now AI notetakers. Many video platforms can transcribe and summarise meetings, depending on your plan and settings. They're genuinely useful for people who missed the call, and for catching action items. But set rules. Announce it at the start and respect anyone who asks to switch it off. Don't use it in one-to-ones, HR, health or disciplinary conversations. Have a named person check the summary before it's shared, because AI can misattribute who said what or invent a decision that wasn't made. And remember recording is subject to privacy law and workplace policy, so check with your data protection lead.
scenes.onScreen:
AI notetakers
• Useful for catch-up and actions
• Announce; allow opt-out
• Not for 1:1s, HR, health, discipline
• Human checks before sharing
• Privacy law and policy apply
scenes.visual: Layout: a meeting window with a small 'transcribing' indicator. 0:00 an AI summary panel fills; 0:20 one line 'Decision: approve budget' flashes red with a note 'not actually decided'; 0:35 a human reviewer icon corrects it; 0:45 a shield icon labelled 'privacy and policy'.

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I'm designing a one-hour meeting for an illustrative product launch decision. Purpose: decide. Outcome: by the end, we will have chosen launch date A or B. Pre-read: a two-page comparison, sent tomorrow morning, with three questions. Agenda: ten minutes silent read, twenty minutes risks for each option, fifteen minutes decision, fifteen minutes actions and comms. Attendees: two deciders, three inputs. I cut two people who only need to be informed and add them to the summary list. Decision rule: the product director decides after hearing input. I paste the card into the invite.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me: meeting design card
• Purpose: decide
• Outcome: date A or B
• Pre-read + 3 questions
• Timed agenda
• 2 deciders, 3 inputs, 2 informed
• Decision rule named
scenes.visual: Layout: screen-recording style calendar invite. 0:00 the design-card fields fill in; 0:25 a timed agenda table appears; 0:40 two attendee chips move from 'invited' to 'informed afterwards'; 0:55 the decision-rule line highlights; 1:05 'Send' button pressed.

scenes.narration: How do you measure whether meetings are improving? Track a few simple signals. Hours per person per week in meetings. The percentage of meetings with a written outcome. How many decisions carry an owner and a date. And ask attendees a one-question pulse at the end of the month: which meeting would you cancel, and why? You'll be surprised how honest people are. Then act on it. A calendar audit every quarter keeps meeting creep in check.
scenes.onScreen:
Measuring success
• Meeting hours per person
• % with a written outcome
• Decisions with owner + date
• 'Which meeting would you cancel?'
• Quarterly calendar audit
scenes.visual: Layout: four KPI tiles. 0:00 'hours per person' falling line; 0:12 'written outcome' percentage ring filling; 0:24 'owner and date' tick counter; 0:36 a pulse-survey bubble 'Which meeting would you cancel?'; 0:48 a calendar with a quarterly repeating audit marker.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Meetings with no stated purpose. Information-only meetings that should be emails. Inviting everyone just in case. No pre-read, or a pre-read nobody reads. Letting the loudest voice dominate. Ending without owners and dates. Hybrid meetings where remote people are an afterthought. And treating an unchecked AI summary as the official record of what was decided.
scenes.onScreen:

• Updates as meetings
• Everyone invited
• Unread pre-reads
• Loudest voice wins
• No owners or dates
• Remote afterthought
• Unchecked AI summary
scenes.visual: Layout: eight mistake cards arranged as a calendar week, each card turning red in sequence every four seconds; 0:35 the final card shows an AI summary with a red 'unverified' stamp.

scenes.narration: Let's recap. Every meeting needs one purpose and a written outcome. Design it with an agenda, the right people and a pre-read. Run it on time, with fair participation and a parking lot. Close with decisions, owners, dates and communication. Set clear rules for AI notetakers. Your try this now: do the fifteen-minute calendar audit in the lesson, and cancel, shorten or convert at least one recurring meeting to an async update this month. Next, we'll look at writing: how to write messages that busy people actually read.

keyTakeaways: Only meet when real-time discussion is needed; use written updates for information.
Design meetings with a purpose, desired outcome, right participants, agenda and pre-read.
Run with clear roles, inclusive facilitation and a parking lot; close with who/what/when.
Audit recurring meetings and design hybrid meetings to include remote participants fairly.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which situation is best handled without a meeting?
options: Resolving a conflict between team members
Deciding between two suppliers with trade-offs
Sharing a routine weekly status update

knowledgeCheck.question: What should every meeting end with?

Clear decisions and actions with owners and deadlines

Go round the table or have people write ideas before discussion

lessons.title: Writing that gets read and acted on
lessons.body:
### Busy readers skim

Most business messages are read quickly on a phone, between meetings. If the key point is buried in paragraph four, it may never be read. Clear writing respects the reader's time and gets the result you need.

### Bottom line up front (BLUF)

Start with the conclusion, request or decision needed. Then provide supporting detail.

| Buried lead | BLUF |
|---|---|
| "Following our discussions last month about the warehouse project, and after reviewing several options with the team, considering costs and timelines, we believe that... [paragraph 3] ...so we need approval by Friday." | "**Request:** Please approve the extra 50,000 for the warehouse racking by Friday, so installation can start on schedule. **Why:** The original quote excluded seismic bracing required by the new code. **Options considered:** see below." |

### The pyramid principle

Barbara Minto's **pyramid principle** structures documents with the main idea at the top, supported by a small number of key arguments, each supported by evidence. It mirrors how readers want to absorb information: answer first, then reasons.

```
Main point: We should launch in Saudi Arabia before the UAE.
  ├─ Reason 1: Larger addressable market for our product category
  │     └─ Evidence: market data, customer interviews
  ├─ Reason 2: Existing distribution partner ready in Riyadh
  │     └─ Evidence: signed letter of intent
  └─ Reason 3: Regulatory approval timeline is shorter for our category
        └─ Evidence: regulator guidance, adviser opinion
```

### Techniques for clarity

- **One message per email** where possible; use clear subject lines ("Decision needed by Fri: warehouse racking budget").
- **Short sentences and paragraphs.** Aim for one idea per paragraph.
- **Plain language:** "use" instead of "utilise"; avoid jargon or define it.
- **Active voice:** "The team completed testing" rather than "Testing was completed".
- **Headings and bullets** for scanning.
- **Specific numbers and dates:** "by 14:00 Thursday" rather than "ASAP".
- **Make the ask explicit:** what do you need, from whom, by when?

### Editing checklist

```
[ ] Is the main point or request in the first two lines?
[ ] Would the subject line alone tell the reader what is needed?
[ ] Can any sentence be removed without losing meaning?
[ ] Are there words the reader might not know?
[ ] Are actions, owners and dates explicit?
[ ] Is the tone appropriate for the reader and the culture?
[ ] Have I checked names, numbers and attachments?
```

### Tone and culture

Tone that seems efficient in one culture may seem abrupt in another. In many Gulf and South Asian business contexts, a courteous greeting and relationship-building line are expected before the business point; in many US contexts, brevity is valued. BLUF still works: a short courteous opening followed immediately by the key point. When in doubt, mirror the style of the person you are writing to.

### Writing with AI assistants

AI tools can draft, shorten and polish messages quickly. Use them to produce a first draft or to simplify complex text, then check facts, tone and confidentiality. Do not paste sensitive information into tools your organisation has not approved, and remember that you are responsible for what you send.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* An analyst at a fictional bank in London sent a six-paragraph email about a data issue; the manager missed the request for approval at the end, and a regulatory report was delayed. After training, the analyst rewrote similar emails with a subject line "Approval needed today: correction to Q2 data submission", a two-line summary, and details below. Response times improved markedly.

### Hands-on: BLUF template, before/after rewrite and an AI editing prompt

**1. BLUF template for any message over five lines:**

```text
Subject: [Decision needed / FYI / Action] — topic — by [date]

Bottom line: [the one sentence the reader must take away, or the decision you need]
Why: [2–3 bullets with the key reasons or evidence]
What I need from you: [specific action] by [date/time]
Details (optional): [background, options considered, links]
```

**2. Before and after (illustrative):**

```text
BEFORE: "Hi all, following on from last week's discussions and several conversations
with the vendor, I've been looking into the various options around the CRM renewal..."
(the ask appears in paragraph four)

AFTER:
Subject: Decision needed — CRM renewal — by Thursday 5 pm
Bottom line: I recommend renewing for 12 months, not 36, at the vendor's revised price.
Why: • Two alternatives are being evaluated by IT this quarter
     • The 36-month discount does not cover the switching risk
What I need: Approve or reject by Thursday 5 pm; silence = I'll escalate Friday.
```

**3. AI editing prompt** (edit your own draft; keep confidential data out of unapproved tools):

```text
Edit this message for a busy senior reader. Put the bottom line first, cut it by
at least 30% without losing facts, use plain British English, keep my tone
[friendly/formal], and list any claims that need a source. Do not add facts.
[paste draft]
```

Then read the AI version aloud once. If it sounds like nobody you know, put your voice back in.

### Common mistakes

- Burying the request.
- Long, dense paragraphs.
- Several unrelated topics in one message.
- Vague deadlines.
- Reply-all to large groups for one-to-one matters.

### Quick self-check

Take the last important email you sent. Rewrite its first two lines in BLUF format and compare. Would the reader have acted faster on the new version?

### Writing for different formats

Chat messages should be even shorter: one point, one ask. Reports and proposals need an executive summary of no more than a page, followed by sections that each answer one question. Slides should carry headlines, not paragraphs. Whatever the format, apply the same test: can the reader find the main point and the required action within seconds?

scenes.narration: Here's an uncomfortable truth. Most of the people who receive your emails, chat messages and documents won't read them fully. They'll skim the first line or two, decide whether it matters, and move on. If your key point is in paragraph four, it may as well not exist. In this lecture you'll learn how to write for skimmers: bottom line up front, the pyramid principle, practical techniques for clarity, how tone shifts across cultures, and how to use AI assistants to edit without losing your voice. By the end, you'll rewrite one real message.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because most work now happens in writing. Email, chat, tickets, documents and proposals. Remote and hybrid teams depend on it even more. Unclear writing costs time: follow-up questions, misunderstandings, and decisions made on the wrong assumption. Clear writing is also a signal of clear thinking. Senior people notice who can explain a complex issue in a few lines. That's often who gets trusted with the next big piece of work.
scenes.onScreen:
Why it matters
• Work happens in writing
• Unclear = questions, errors, delays
• Clear writing signals clear thinking
• It gets you trusted
scenes.visual: Layout: a message thread. 0:00 an unclear message leads to a chain of five question replies; 0:20 a second thread with a clear message gets one 'Approved' reply; 0:35 a small spotlight falls on the clear writer's avatar.

scenes.narration: Here's the concept. BLUF, bottom line up front, comes from military writing. Put the conclusion, recommendation or request first, then the supporting reasons, then the detail. The pyramid principle, developed by Barbara Minto, formalises this: start with the main point, group supporting arguments beneath it, and support each with evidence. Here's the key idea. Write in the order the reader needs, not the order you discovered things. Your discovery journey is interesting to you. Your reader wants the destination.
scenes.onScreen:
BLUF and the pyramid
• Bottom line first
• Then reasons
• Then detail
• Minto's pyramid principle
• Reader's order, not discovery order
scenes.visual: Layout: a pyramid. 0:00 the top block 'Main point' drops in; 0:10 three blocks beneath 'Reason 1, 2, 3'; 0:20 a base row of evidence blocks; 0:35 a winding path labelled 'your discovery journey' fades, replaced by a straight arrow to the top.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a newspaper story. The headline tells you what happened. The first paragraph tells you who, what, where and when. Each later paragraph adds detail you can skip if you're busy. Editors call it the inverted pyramid, and it's designed for readers who might stop at any moment. Your emails should work the same way. If your reader stops after the subject line, do they know what you need? After the first sentence, do they know the answer?
scenes.onScreen:
The newspaper test
• Headline = subject line
• First paragraph = bottom line
• Later paragraphs = skippable detail
• Could they stop at any point?

scenes.narration: Now some techniques for clarity. Use a subject line that says what kind of message this is and when a response is needed, like decision needed, CRM renewal, by Thursday. Keep sentences short, and use one idea per paragraph. Prefer plain words: use rather than utilise, help rather than facilitate. Use the active voice: the team missed the deadline, rather than the deadline was missed. Use bullets for lists, and bold sparingly for the one thing people mustn't miss. And make the ask specific: what you need, from whom, by when.
scenes.onScreen:
Clarity techniques
• Informative subject lines
• Short sentences, one idea per paragraph
• Plain words, active voice
• Bullets for lists
• Specific asks: what, who, when
scenes.visual: Layout: a 'before' sentence on screen: 'Facilitation of the utilisation of the platform was undertaken.' 0:10 words strike through and rewrite to 'We helped the team use the platform.'; 0:25 a subject line builds with three tags; 0:40 an ask card with three fields.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Mehwish, a project coordinator in Karachi, needs her manager to approve an extra freelancer. Her first draft begins: Hi, hope you're well. As you know, we've been having a busy few weeks, and there have been a few challenges. The ask is at the bottom. She rewrites it. Subject: approval needed, one extra freelancer, by Wednesday. First line: I'd like approval to hire one freelancer for three weeks at the agreed day rate to keep the client launch on time. Then three bullets of reasons. Her manager approves it in four minutes.

• Rewrite: subject says 'approval needed'
• First line = the request
• 3 bullets of reasons
• Approved in 4 minutes

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. At a consumer goods company in Dubai, the regional marketing lead, Rashid, sends a monthly performance report to the country managers. It's twelve pages. Almost nobody replies, and the same questions keep coming up in meetings. He restructures it. Page one is a BLUF summary: three things that changed, one decision needed from each country, and a traffic-light table. The detail moves to an appendix. Replies go from almost none to most of the country managers within a week, and the monthly meeting drops by thirty minutes.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 2: Rashid in Dubai (illustrative)
• 12-page report, few replies
• Page one: 3 changes, 1 decision each, traffic lights
• Detail to appendix
• Replies up; meeting 30 minutes shorter

scenes.narration: Tone and culture matter too. In some workplaces, especially in parts of South Asia and the Gulf, a warmer opening and more courtesy are expected, and a message that starts with the ask can feel abrupt. In many UK and US workplaces, brevity is read as respect. You don't have to choose between clarity and courtesy. A one-line greeting followed by the bottom line works almost everywhere. Also consider readers working in a second language: shorter sentences, fewer idioms, and no sarcasm, which rarely survives in writing.
scenes.onScreen:
Tone and culture
• Warmth expected in some cultures
• Brevity = respect in others
• One-line greeting + bottom line
• Second-language readers: short, literal, no sarcasm
scenes.visual: Layout: an email template with an adjustable 'warmth' slider. 0:00 the slider moves and the greeting line lengthens or shortens while the bottom line stays fixed; 0:30 an idiom 'ballpark figure' crosses out and becomes 'rough estimate'.

scenes.narration: Different formats need different shapes. In chat, lead with the point in one message rather than five fragments, and never send just hi, then wait for a reply. Say what you need in the first message. In email, the subject line does half the work. In a document or proposal, add a short executive summary at the top, headings that say something, like costs rise in quarter three, rather than costs, and an appendix for the detail. And for anything sensitive or emotional, writing is usually the wrong format altogether. Pick up the phone or book a call, then confirm in writing.
scenes.onScreen:
Different formats
• Chat: the point in one message, not 'hi'
• Email: the subject does half the work
• Docs: summary + headings that say something
• Sensitive? Talk first, then write
scenes.visual: Layout: three device frames side by side. 0:00 a chat window where five fragment bubbles merge into one clear message; 0:15 an email subject line highlights; 0:30 a document outline where the heading 'Costs' rewrites to 'Costs rise in Q3'; 0:45 a phone icon with 'talk first' appears over a sensitive-topic envelope.

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I take an illustrative draft about a CRM renewal where the ask sits in paragraph four. First, I write the bottom line: I recommend renewing for twelve months, not thirty-six. Then three reasons. Then the ask: approve or reject by Thursday at five. I paste the draft into an AI assistant with the editing prompt from the lesson: bottom line first, cut by thirty per cent, plain British English, no new facts. It shortens it well, but it adds a claim about pricing I never made. I delete that line. Then I read it aloud and put back one phrase that sounds like me.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me: BLUF rewrite + AI edit
• Bottom line first
• 3 reasons, 1 ask with a deadline
• AI trims 30%
• Remove an invented claim
• Read aloud; restore your voice
scenes.visual: Layout: screen-recording style editor. 0:00 a long draft; 0:15 a bottom-line sentence moves to the top; 0:30 a side chat returns a shorter version; 0:40 one sentence highlights red 'not in original' and is deleted; 0:55 a speaker icon plays as the text is read aloud.

scenes.narration: How do you measure clear writing? Look at the responses. Fewer follow-up questions. Faster replies to decision requests. Decisions made on the first round, not the third. You can also test yourself before sending: could someone who reads only the subject and first sentence act correctly? And every so often, ask a trusted colleague to read one of your messages and tell you, in one sentence, what you're asking for. If their sentence doesn't match yours, rewrite.
scenes.onScreen:
Measuring success
• Fewer follow-up questions
• Faster replies
• First-round decisions
• Subject + first sentence test
• A colleague's one-sentence summary
scenes.visual: Layout: a message analytics mock-up. 0:00 a 'follow-up questions' bar falls; 0:12 a 'time to reply' bar shortens; 0:25 a test card 'subject + first sentence: can they act?'; 0:40 two speech bubbles compare the writer's and the reader's one-sentence summaries.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Burying the ask. Vague subject lines like quick question or update. Long paragraphs covering five topics. Jargon and acronyms the reader doesn't know. Passive voice that hides who's responsible. Writing in anger and sending immediately. Copying the whole company when three people need it. And pasting AI-generated text without checking it, which can add facts you never said and a voice that sounds like nobody.

lessons.title: Making better decisions as a group
lessons.body:
### Why group decisions go wrong

Groups can make better decisions than individuals because they combine knowledge and perspectives. But they often fall into predictable traps:

- **Groupthink:** desire for harmony suppresses dissent.
- **Anchoring:** the first number or idea mentioned dominates.
- **Authority bias:** everyone defers to the most senior person.
- **Confirmation bias:** people seek information that supports their existing view.
- **Unclear decision rights:** nobody knows who decides, so decisions drift.

### Step 1: clarify how the decision will be made

Before discussion, state **who decides** and **how**:

| Method | When to use | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Leader decides alone | Urgent, low-impact or confidential | Low buy-in |
| Leader decides after consultation | Most important decisions | Consultation must be genuine |
| Majority vote | Many equal stakeholders, moderate stakes | Losing minority disengages |
| Consensus (all can live with it) | High need for commitment | Slow; can water down decisions |
| Delegate to the group or an individual | Expertise sits with them | Must respect their decision |

Frameworks such as RACI or RAPID (Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide) help make decision rights explicit.

### Step 2: frame the decision well

- What exactly are we deciding? (One sentence.)
- What criteria matter? (Cost, time, risk, customer impact, strategic fit.)
- What options exist? Always generate at least three, including "do nothing".
- What information do we need, and what is good enough given the stakes and time?

### Step 3: improve the discussion

Techniques that reduce bias:

- **Independent input first:** ask people to write their view or estimate before discussion (reduces anchoring and authority bias).
- **Senior people speak last.**
- **Devil's advocate or red team:** someone argues the strongest case against the preferred option.
- **Pre-mortem:** "Imagine it is a year from now and this decision failed. Why?"
- **Separate facts from opinions:** label clearly.

### Step 4: decide and commit

State the decision clearly, including the reasoning and the key trade-offs accepted. Ask for commitment: people may disagree but should support implementation ("disagree and commit"). Record it in a decision log.

```
Decision log entry
Date: 12 March
Decision: Enter Saudi market first; UAE in phase 2
Decided by: CEO after consultation with leadership team
Options considered: KSA first; UAE first; both simultaneously
Key reasons: partner readiness, market size, regulatory timeline
Trade-offs accepted: slower UAE revenue; higher initial travel costs
Dissent noted: CFO preferred UAE first due to lower setup cost
Review point: after 6 months, compare against KPIs
```

### Reversible and irreversible decisions

Distinguish decisions that are easy to reverse (try something, learn, change course) from those that are hard to reverse (major investments, public commitments). Move quickly on reversible decisions; invest more time and analysis in irreversible ones.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* A fictional e-commerce startup in Lahore had to choose a payment provider. In the first meeting, the founder stated a preference, and everyone agreed. A board adviser suggested restarting: each team member independently scored three providers against agreed criteria (fees, reliability, settlement time, support, integration effort). The independent scores revealed that the founder's preferred provider scored poorly on settlement time, which mattered greatly for cash flow. The team chose a different provider, and the founder later described the process as the most useful change to how they made decisions.

### Hands-on: a decision record and a pre-mortem you can run in 20 minutes

**1. One-page decision record** (keep them in a shared folder or wiki so decisions are findable):

```text
DECISION RECORD — [title] — [date]
Decision needed:   (framed as a question with options, not yes/no only)
Decider:           (one named person or body)     Rule: consult / consent / vote / consensus
Input from:        (names/roles)                   Informed: (who hears afterwards)
Type:              one-way door (hard to reverse) | two-way door (easy to reverse)
Options considered: A / B / C with main pros, cons and risks
Evidence:          (data, sources; flag assumptions)
Decision:          
Why:               
Dissent recorded:  (who disagreed and why; "disagree and commit" agreed?)
Review date / signal that would make us revisit:
```

**2. Pre-mortem (20 minutes, from Gary Klein's technique):**

```text
1. "Imagine it's 12 months from now and this decision has failed badly." (1 min)
2. Everyone writes reasons it failed, silently and independently. (5 min)
3. Round-robin: one reason each until all are shared. (7 min)
4. Pick the top 3 risks; agree a mitigation or an early-warning signal for each. (7 min)
```

**3. AI as a devil's advocate** (anonymise sensitive data):

```text
We are about to decide [decision] for [context]. Our preferred option is [A] because [reasons].
Argue the strongest case against A and for the best alternative. List assumptions we
are making that could be wrong and what evidence would test each. Do not decide for us.
```

Use the output to widen the discussion. It is not evidence, and it cannot know your organisation's context.

### Common mistakes

- Starting discussion before clarifying who decides.
- Only one option considered.
- Leader states preference first.
- Endless consensus seeking on low-stakes decisions.
- Decisions not recorded, so they are reopened.

### Quick self-check

Think of your team's last significant decision. Could everyone say who made it, what options were considered and why the chosen option won? If not, use the decision log template next time.

### Decision-making under time pressure

When time is short, decide who decides, set a deadline for input, and accept "good enough" information for reversible choices. Communicate the decision and the reasoning quickly, and schedule a review point. Delaying a decision is itself a decision, often with hidden costs.

### Learning from decisions

Judge decisions by the quality of the process as well as the outcome. A good process can still produce a bad result through bad luck, and a poor process can get lucky. Reviewing decision logs periodically helps teams learn which processes lead to better results over time.

scenes.narration: Have you ever sat in a meeting where everyone nodded along to a decision, and then, in the corridor afterwards, half of them said they thought it was a mistake? That's not a people problem. It's a process problem. Groups can make much better decisions than individuals, because they bring more information and perspectives. But only if you design the process. In this lecture, you'll learn why group decisions go wrong, how to clarify who decides and how, how to frame and discuss a decision well, and how to decide and commit, including using a pre-mortem.

scenes.narration: Why does it matter? Because the quality of a team's decisions compounds. A slightly better choice on priorities, hiring, pricing or suppliers, made again and again, adds up to a very different business over a year. And groups have well-known traps. Groupthink, where the desire for harmony suppresses disagreement. Anchoring on the first idea mentioned. The most senior or loudest person steering the room. And endless debate with no clear decider. Each of these has a practical fix.

scenes.narration: Here's the first concept. Before discussing the content, clarify the process. Who decides? One person, a small group, or everyone? And what's the rule? Consult, where the decider hears input and then decides. Consent, where the proposal goes ahead unless someone has a reasoned objection. Vote. Or full consensus, which is slow and best kept for decisions everyone must live with deeply. Frameworks such as RAPID, from Bain, or DACI, used in many product teams, name the roles explicitly. Here's the key idea: most decision conflict is really confusion about who decides.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a jury, a referee and a family choosing a holiday. A jury must reach a verdict by a defined rule. A referee decides alone, instantly, after taking in what they can see. A family discusses, but in the end one or two people book the flights. Each is a legitimate way to decide. Chaos comes when people think they're on a jury, but actually there's a referee. Tell people which game they're playing before the discussion starts.

Instead of a yes or no question, like should we launch in Saudi Arabia, frame it with options: which market should we enter next, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, or deepen the UAE? That invites real comparison. scenes.narration: Then decide and commit. Distinguish between one-way doors and two-way doors, a phrase popularised by Amazon's shareholder letters. A two-way door is a decision that's easy to reverse: decide fast, learn, adjust. A one-way door is hard to reverse: slow down and do more work. Once the decision is made, ask for disagree and commit. People can disagree openly during the discussion, but once it's decided, everyone supports it fully. Record dissent, and set a review date or a signal that would make you revisit.

modules.title: Stakeholders and influence
modules.summary: Map and manage stakeholders, influence people you do not manage, and build a productive relationship with your own manager.

lessons.title: Stakeholder management
lessons.body:
### Why stakeholders matter

Your success rarely depends only on your own team. Customers, peers in other departments, senior leaders, suppliers, regulators and partners all affect whether your work succeeds. **Stakeholder management** is the deliberate practice of understanding these people and engaging them effectively.

### Step 1: identify stakeholders

Ask: Who is affected by our work? Who can influence it? Who has resources we need? Who could block us? Who has expertise we need? List individuals, not just departments, because relationships are with people.

### Step 2: map them

The **power–interest grid** is a quick start:

| | Low interest | High interest |
|---|---|---|
| **High power** | Keep satisfied: brief, focused updates; consult on major decisions | Manage closely: involve early and often |
| **Low power** | Monitor: light-touch updates | Keep informed: regular communication; they can become allies or critics |

Then add depth for key people: What do they care about? What are their goals and pressures? How do they prefer to communicate? What is their current attitude toward your work, and what would you like it to be?

### Stakeholder profile template

```
Name / role: Head of Sales, Gulf region
Power: High (budget and sales team priorities)   Interest: Medium
Cares about: Quarterly targets, key account relationships
Concerns about our initiative: Sales team time spent on new CRM training
Communication preference: Short WhatsApp/Teams messages; face-to-face monthly
Current stance: Neutral        Desired: Supportive champion
Engagement plan: Show pilot results from Dubai team (time saved per rep);
                 schedule training outside quarter-end; invite to steering group
Owner: Programme lead
```

### Step 3: engage

- **Engage early.** People support what they help create.
- **Listen first.** Understand their interests before presenting your solution.
- **Tailor the message.** Executives want outcomes and risks; users want to know what changes for them.
- **Close the loop.** Show how their input shaped decisions.
- **Be consistent.** Say the same thing to different audiences (framed appropriately); inconsistency destroys trust.

### Step 4: review and adapt

Stakeholders change: new leaders arrive, priorities shift, early supporters lose interest. Review your map monthly for important initiatives.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Ali, a programme lead at a fictional FMCG company in Karachi, was rolling out a new demand planning process. He mapped 20 stakeholders and discovered that regional sales managers, whom he had placed as "low interest", actually controlled the data the new process needed. He moved them to "manage closely", visited three regional offices, and co-designed a simpler data template with them. Data quality improved, and the sales managers became advocates when the process went live.

### Stakeholders outside the organisation

External stakeholders, such as customers, regulators and communities, require extra care. Communications may be public or legally significant; involve legal, compliance or communications colleagues where appropriate. Be accurate and avoid overpromising.

### Hands-on: build a stakeholder map and engagement plan in a spreadsheet

Create a sheet (Google Sheets, Excel or a Notion table) with these columns. Score power and interest from 1 to 5.

| Stakeholder | Role | Power (1–5) | Interest (1–5) | Quadrant | Current stance | Desired stance | What they care about | Concerns | Channel & frequency | Owner | Last contact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Finance director | Budget approver | 5 | 3 | Keep satisfied | Neutral | Supportive | Payback < 18 months | Hidden run costs | Monthly 1-page note | Me | 2 Sep |
| Store managers | Users | 2 | 5 | Keep informed | Sceptical | Supportive | Less admin at peak | Training time | Fortnightly update + pilot | Aisha | 5 Sep |

Add a formula so the quadrant fills itself (Google Sheets / Excel):

```text
=IF(AND(C2>=3,D2>=3),"Manage closely",IF(C2>=3,"Keep satisfied",IF(D2>=3,"Keep informed","Monitor")))
```

Then add conditional formatting on "Last contact" to highlight anyone not contacted in 30 days:

```text
Custom formula (applied to column L):  =TODAY()-$L2>30
```

**Monthly 15-minute review:** sort by quadrant, check stance gaps (current vs desired), and pick the three people you will speak to this month.

**Optional AI prompt** (roles only, no personal data):

```text
Here is an anonymised stakeholder list for a project to [goal] with roles, power,
interest and concerns. Which stakeholders might I have missed? For the three
"manage closely" roles, suggest what evidence each is likely to need and one
question I should ask them. Flag assumptions.
```

### Common mistakes

- Mapping stakeholders once and never updating.
- Focusing only on senior stakeholders and ignoring influential people at other levels.
- Broadcasting information instead of engaging in dialogue.
- Different messages to different groups that contradict each other.
- Ignoring critics instead of understanding their concerns.

### Quick self-check

Name the three stakeholders whose support you most need this quarter. For each, write what they care about most. If you are unsure, schedule a conversation to find out.

### Handling difficult stakeholders

Some stakeholders are sceptical, demanding or hostile. Start by understanding why: they may have been let down before, may fear losing control or resources, or may simply lack information. Meet them one-to-one, listen without defending, and ask what would make the initiative acceptable to them. Look for small commitments you can keep reliably, because trust with sceptics is built through evidence, not persuasion. If a stakeholder continues to block progress unreasonably, escalate through your sponsor with a clear description of the impact and the options, rather than engaging in a public dispute.

### A monthly stakeholder review

For important initiatives, spend thirty minutes each month reviewing your map: who has changed role, whose attitude has shifted, who has been neglected, and which relationships need investment. Update your engagement plan accordingly. This small routine prevents many unpleasant surprises, particularly during long programmes where leadership changes are common.

### Quick check

Ask yourself: which stakeholder would be most surprised by our next decision? Talk to them first.

scenes.narration: Here's a pattern you may recognise. A project is going well. The team is delivering. And then, three weeks before launch, someone you barely thought about, a finance director, a regional head, a legal adviser, raises an objection that stops everything. Most projects don't fail for technical reasons. They stall because the right people weren't involved at the right time. In this lecture, you'll learn how to identify stakeholders, map them by power and interest, engage each group appropriately, and review your map as things change. By the end, you'll have a working stakeholder map.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because stakeholders control the things your work depends on: budget, approvals, people, data and adoption. A stakeholder who feels consulted is far more likely to help you. One who feels surprised is far more likely to resist, even if your idea is good. Stakeholder management isn't politics in the negative sense. It's respecting that other people have legitimate interests and giving them the right information at the right time.

scenes.narration: Here's the concept. Step one, identify stakeholders widely. Think about who's affected, who decides, who influences the deciders, who has the expertise, and who might block. Include people outside the organisation too: clients, suppliers, regulators. Step two, map them on a simple grid. Power on one axis, meaning their ability to affect the outcome. Interest on the other, meaning how much they care. This is often called the power-interest grid, associated with Mendelow. Here's the key idea: different quadrants need different engagement, and treating everyone the same wastes time and annoys people.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of planning a wedding. The couple's parents are high power and high interest: you consult them closely. The venue manager has high power, but mainly cares about logistics: keep them satisfied with clear information. Distant cousins are very interested but have little say: keep them informed with a nice update. The neighbours: just let them know about the parking. If you consulted distant cousins on the menu and forgot to tell the venue, you'd have chaos. Projects work exactly the same way.
scenes.onScreen:
The wedding planner
• Parents: manage closely
• Venue: keep satisfied
• Cousins: keep informed
• Neighbours: monitor
scenes.visual: Layout: the 2x2 grid again with illustrated wedding figures placed in each quadrant. 0:00 parents in top right; 0:10 venue manager top left; 0:20 cousins bottom right; 0:30 neighbours bottom left with a parking sign; 0:40 a chaotic version swaps them and shows confusion icons.

scenes.narration: Step three, engage. For manage closely, involve them early in shaping the work, meet regularly and ask for their input on key decisions. For keep satisfied, give concise, relevant updates focused on what they care about, such as cost, risk or compliance, and don't overload them. For keep informed, share regular updates and invite feedback, because they're often your users and your early warning system. For monitor, a light touch. And for each key stakeholder, note what they care about, their concerns, and their current and desired stance. The gap between those is your engagement plan.
scenes.onScreen:
Engage
• Manage closely: shape together
• Keep satisfied: concise, their priorities
• Keep informed: updates + feedback
• Monitor: light touch
• Current vs desired stance = plan
scenes.visual: Layout: four quadrant cards expand one at a time, each revealing its engagement method with a small icon: handshake, one-page note, newsletter, eye. 0:40 a stance bar for one stakeholder shows 'neutral' moving to 'supportive' with an arrow labelled 'plan'.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Adnan, an IT lead at a college in Lahore, wants to move all staff to a new learning platform. He maps stakeholders. The principal: high power, medium interest, keep satisfied with a cost and risk summary. Heads of department: high power, high interest, manage closely through a design workshop. Teachers: high interest, lower power, keep informed and invite them to a pilot. Students: keep informed. The IT support contractor: keep satisfied. Because heads of department helped design the rollout, they champion it, and adoption is much smoother than the last system change.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 1: Adnan's college (illustrative)
• Principal: keep satisfied
• Heads of department: manage closely
• Teachers: keep informed + pilot
• Contractor: keep satisfied
• Heads become champions
scenes.visual: Layout: the power-interest grid populated with the college roles. 0:00 roles drop in one by one; 0:30 heads of department glow and move to a workshop table icon; 0:45 a champion badge appears on them; 0:55 an adoption meter rises.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. Layla is rolling out a new inventory system across twenty stores for a fashion retailer in Abu Dhabi. She maps stakeholders in a spreadsheet. The finance director cares about payback and hidden running costs: she sends a one-page monthly note with those exact numbers. Store managers are sceptical because peak season is coming: she runs a pilot in two stores and brings their feedback into the design. The legal team cares about data handling: she involves them before choosing the vendor. Launch is on time, and the store managers present the pilot results to their peers.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 2: Layla in Abu Dhabi (illustrative)
• 20 stores, new inventory system
• Finance: payback note monthly
• Store managers: pilot + feedback
• Legal: early on data handling
• Managers present results to peers
scenes.visual: Layout: a spreadsheet with stakeholder rows. 0:00 rows fill; 0:20 a one-page note icon travels to 'Finance'; 0:35 a two-store pilot map lights up; 0:50 a legal shield icon attaches to the vendor selection step; 1:05 store-manager avatars present to a room.

scenes.narration: Step four, review and adapt. Stakeholders move. A reorganisation brings in a new director. A budget cut makes finance far more interested. A project phase shifts attention from IT to operations. So review your map monthly, in fifteen minutes. Who has moved? Where's the biggest gap between current and desired stance? Who haven't you spoken to in a month? Pick three people to talk to this month. And watch for silent stakeholders: people who are affected but never speak up, often frontline staff. Silence isn't support.
scenes.onScreen:
Review and adapt
• Stakeholders move
• Monthly 15-minute review
• Biggest stance gap
• Who's gone quiet?
• Silence isn't support
scenes.visual: Layout: the grid animates over three monthly frames; 0:00 frame one; 0:12 a 'new director' icon lands; 0:24 'finance' slides from low to high interest; 0:36 a quiet frontline icon pulses with a caption 'silence isn't support'.

scenes.narration: What about a genuinely difficult stakeholder, someone powerful who seems to oppose everything? Start by assuming they have a reason. Meet them one to one, early, and ask: what would need to be true for you to support this? What worries you most? Often the objection is about a risk they own, like compliance, budget or their team's workload, and you can design around it. Involve them in solving that part. If they still disagree, make sure their concern is recorded and escalated fairly to the decider, not ignored. People can accept losing an argument. They rarely accept being bypassed.
scenes.onScreen:
Difficult stakeholders
• Assume there's a reason
• Meet early, one to one
• 'What would need to be true?'
• Design around the risk they own
• Record and escalate fairly; never bypass
scenes.visual: Layout: a stakeholder icon with crossed arms. 0:00 a one-to-one table appears; 0:12 a question bubble 'What would need to be true?'; 0:25 a hidden risk card 'compliance' flips; 0:40 a design change wraps around the risk; 0:55 the arms uncross, or a 'concern recorded' document travels to a decider icon.

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I open a spreadsheet for an illustrative project, launching a client self-service portal. I list twelve stakeholders by role and score power and interest from one to five. I add the quadrant formula from the lesson, so the quadrant fills itself. Then conditional formatting to highlight anyone I haven't contacted in thirty days. Two cells turn red: the head of legal and the customer service team leads. Then I ask an AI assistant, with roles only, who I might have missed. It suggests the accessibility lead and the data protection officer. Good catch. I add both.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me: spreadsheet stakeholder map
• Score power and interest
• Quadrant formula
• 30-day contact highlight
• AI: who have I missed?
• Add accessibility + data protection
scenes.visual: Layout: screen-recording style spreadsheet. 0:00 rows type in; 0:20 the quadrant column populates via formula; 0:35 two last-contact cells turn red; 0:50 a side chat suggests two new roles; 1:00 two new rows are added.

scenes.narration: How do you measure success? Look for fewer surprises late in the project. Faster approvals. Stakeholders moving from sceptical or neutral towards supportive. And people raising concerns early, directly with you, rather than in a steering committee. You can even add a simple column to your sheet for stance, and track the count of supportive key stakeholders over time. If it's not moving, change your engagement approach, not just the frequency of your emails.
scenes.onScreen:
Measuring success
• Fewer late surprises
• Faster approvals
• Stance moving to supportive
• Concerns raised early, directly
• Change approach, not email volume
scenes.visual: Layout: a line chart 'supportive key stakeholders' rising over months. 0:00 line draws; 0:15 a 'late surprises' bar shrinks; 0:30 an approval-time clock shortens; 0:45 an email-volume icon with a caption 'more emails isn't a strategy'.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Only thinking about senior stakeholders and forgetting users. Treating everyone the same, so senior people get overloaded and users get ignored. Engaging people only when you need something. Surprising powerful people in public meetings. Assuming silence means agreement. Letting the map go stale after week one. And pasting personal notes about named individuals into an AI tool. Keep stakeholder analysis professional and role-based, especially if it could ever be read by the people it describes.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Forgetting users
• Same approach for all
• Only when you need something
• Public surprises
• Silence = agreement
• Stale maps
• Personal notes in AI tools
scenes.visual: Layout: seven warning cards appear on the grid, each pinned to the quadrant it affects, one every five seconds; 0:40 the last card shows a note document with a lock icon 'role-based and professional'.

scenes.narration: Let's recap. Identify stakeholders widely, including those outside the organisation. Map them by power and interest. Engage each quadrant differently, and plan from the gap between current and desired stance. Review monthly, because stakeholders move. Your try this now: build the spreadsheet map from the lesson for your most important project, add the quadrant formula and the thirty-day highlight, and pick three people to talk to this month. Next, we'll look at how to influence people when you don't have authority over them.
scenes.onScreen:
Recap and try this now
• Identify widely
• Power-interest map
• Engage by quadrant
• Review monthly
• Action: build the sheet; 3 conversations

Engage early, listen first, tailor messages and show how input shaped decisions.
Keep messages consistent across audiences and review stakeholder maps regularly.
Take extra care with external stakeholders such as customers and regulators.
