The working agreement + cadence
• Overlap hours
• Channels and response times
• Meeting norms, status, decisions
• Focus time, time off, AI tools
• Cadence: weekly update, team call, 1:1s, quarterly retro

scenes.narration: Trust at a distance needs deliberate effort. You don't bump into people, so create moments for connection: a few minutes of non-work conversation at the start of calls, virtual coffee pairings, and meeting in person when budgets allow, especially at the start of a project. Be reliable and responsive. Share context generously, because people fill information gaps with worst-case assumptions. And be careful with surveillance tools that track keystrokes or screens. They signal distrust, can raise legal issues, and usually measure activity rather than results.

• Meet in person when you can
• Be reliable and responsive
• Share context generously
• Avoid surveillance tools

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Hamza leads a four-person design team split between Karachi and Manchester. Messages fly at all hours and people feel always on. He runs a one-hour session where the team writes a working agreement. They set a three-hour overlap window, agree that chat outside those hours gets a reply the next working day, and create a weekly written update on Thursdays. Within a month, late-night messages drop sharply, and designers say they finally have time to focus.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. Noor leads a twenty-person customer success team for a software company, with people in Riyadh, Dubai, Cairo and London. In a hybrid set-up, the Dubai office staff get quick answers and interesting projects because they're near the director. Remote colleagues feel sidelined. Noor introduces rules: all decisions recorded in a shared log, everyone joins meetings from their own device, stretch projects advertised to the whole team, and meeting times rotated. After two quarters, engagement scores among remote members rise and two remote colleagues lead major accounts.

scenes.narration: Fairness and wellbeing need your attention in hybrid teams. Proximity bias is real: people who are physically near leaders tend to get more information, more visibility and more opportunities. Counter it deliberately. And protect wellbeing. Remote work can blur boundaries, so model healthy habits: don't send messages late at night that imply urgency, respect weekends in each country, which may differ, and encourage real time off. Some countries also have legal rules on working time and the right to disconnect, so check yours.

• Respect local weekends
• Check working-time laws

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I draft an illustrative working agreement for a team across London, Dubai and Lahore. First, the overlap: I calculate three hours when all three are at work, and I remember that daylight saving in the UK shifts it for part of the year. Channels: urgent means a call, chat gets a same-day reply, email two days. Focus time: Tuesday and Thursday mornings. AI tools: our approved assistant only, no client data elsewhere, meeting notes announced and checked. Then I share it as a draft and ask the team to comment by Friday. It's theirs, not mine.

• Calculate overlap (mind daylight saving)
• Channels and reply times
• Focus time
• AI tool rules
• Share as a draft for comments

scenes.narration: How do you measure success? Watch a few signals. Are people clear on priorities without asking? Are response-time expectations met without late-night messages? Is information equal for remote and office staff? What do engagement or pulse surveys say, split by location? And are delivery outcomes steady or improving? Ask in your quarterly retrospective: what's one thing in our working agreement that isn't working? Then change it. The agreement is a living document.
scenes.onScreen:
Measuring success
• Priorities clear
• Response times met, no late nights
• Equal information by location
• Pulse surveys split by location
• Delivery outcomes

lessons.title: Communicating across cultures
lessons.body:
### Culture shapes communication

In international and diverse teams, misunderstandings often come not from what is said but from how it is said and interpreted. Culture influences directness, attitudes to hierarchy, how decisions are made, how trust is built and how time is treated.

### Useful dimensions

Researchers such as Erin Meyer (*The Culture Map*) describe scales on which cultures differ. Individuals vary widely, so treat these as starting hypotheses, not stereotypes.

| Dimension | One end | Other end |
|---|---|---|
| Communicating | Low-context: explicit, literal, repetition welcomed | High-context: implicit, nuanced, read between the lines |
| Evaluating (negative feedback) | Direct | Indirect |
| Leading | Egalitarian | Hierarchical |
| Deciding | Consensual | Top-down |
| Trusting | Task-based (trust through work) | Relationship-based (trust through personal connection) |
| Disagreeing | Open confrontation acceptable | Confrontation avoided |
| Scheduling | Linear time (fixed, punctual) | Flexible time |

For example, relationship-based trust is often important in business in the Gulf and South Asia: time spent over coffee or a meal is not a distraction but part of the work. In many US workplaces, trust may be built faster through reliable task delivery. The UK is often described as relatively egalitarian but indirect in delivering criticism, which can confuse colleagues from more direct cultures. Always check with individuals.

### Practical habits

1. **Be explicit in multicultural teams.** Confirm understanding: "To make sure I explained clearly, what are the next steps as you understand them?"
2. **Summarise decisions in writing**, especially across languages.
3. **Avoid idioms, slang and sarcasm** that do not translate.
4. **Ask about preferences:** "How do you prefer to receive feedback?"
5. **Watch for silence:** in some cultures silence means disagreement or discomfort, not agreement.
6. **Respect religious and cultural practices:** prayer times, fasting during Ramadan, different weekends and holidays.
7. **Adapt, but stay authentic:** adjust style while keeping your values consistent.

### Language and fairness

In teams where many people work in a second language, native speakers can dominate. Slow down, use simple language, invite written input, and give people time to respond. Written pre-reads help non-native speakers prepare.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* A UK-based manager at a fictional engineering firm led a team with members in Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. In meetings, she asked, "Any concerns?" and heard none, then discovered problems late. She learned that team members were reluctant to raise concerns openly in front of a senior manager. She began asking specific questions ("What might delay the survey work?"), invited written input before meetings, and held short one-to-ones. Issues surfaced earlier, and team members said they felt more respected.

### Cultural intelligence (CQ)

Cultural intelligence is the capability to work effectively across cultures. It involves:

- **Drive:** motivation to learn and adapt.
- **Knowledge:** understanding cultural differences.
- **Strategy:** planning and checking assumptions in cross-cultural interactions.
- **Action:** adapting behaviour appropriately.

It can be developed through exposure, reflection and feedback.

### Hands-on: a team culture map and a "how I work" profile

**1. Team culture map (run it as a 45-minute team session).** Each person places themselves on each scale, 1–10, privately first, then you discuss the spread. Scales adapted from widely used cross-cultural frameworks such as Erin Meyer's *The Culture Map*:

```text
Communicating:   low-context (explicit, literal)      1 ... 10  high-context (implicit, read between lines)
Feedback:        direct negative feedback             1 ... 10  indirect, softened, private
Deciding:        consensual                           1 ... 10  top-down
Trusting:        task-based (trust from delivery)     1 ... 10  relationship-based (trust from time together)
Disagreeing:     open debate is healthy                1 ... 10  avoid open confrontation
Scheduling:      linear time, deadlines fixed          1 ... 10  flexible time, adapt as needed
```

Discuss: where are we far apart? What misunderstandings has that caused? What will we agree as a team norm (for example, "feedback is private and specific; we say explicitly when a deadline is fixed")?

**2. A personal "how I work" profile** (each person writes one; share in the team space):

```text
Best way to reach me / reply times:
How I like to receive feedback:
How I show disagreement (and how you'll know):
Working days, time zone, public holidays and religious observances I'd like colleagues to know about:
Language notes (e.g. English is my second language; please avoid idioms in writing):
```

**3. Using AI translation carefully.** Translation and live captions in chat and meeting tools help, but check important messages with a fluent colleague, avoid idioms and sarcasm in the source text, and never rely on machine translation for contracts, HR matters or safety instructions.

Remember: frameworks describe tendencies across groups, not individuals. Always ask the person in front of you.

### Common mistakes

- Assuming your own norms are universal.
- Stereotyping individuals based on nationality.
- Interpreting silence as agreement.
- Using humour or idioms that exclude people.
- Scheduling key meetings on others' religious holidays or weekends.

### Quick self-check

Think of a cross-cultural misunderstanding you experienced. Which dimension from the table explains it? What would you do differently next time?

### Worked example: feedback across cultures

*Illustrative.* A US-based sales director gave direct feedback to a new account manager in Riyadh in front of the team: "This proposal is not good enough." The account manager was deeply embarrassed and became withdrawn. A colleague explained that public criticism, especially from a senior person, could cause serious loss of face. The director apologised privately, then moved to private, specific feedback, beginning with appreciation of the relationship and the effort involved before discussing improvements. The account manager's confidence and performance recovered. The lesson was not that direct feedback is wrong, but that setting and framing matter enormously.

### Building a shared team culture

Multicultural teams can create their own "third culture": explicit norms that everyone agrees, such as how to give feedback, how to disagree, and how decisions are made. Discuss preferences openly early in the team's life, write the agreements down, and revisit them when new members join. This reduces the burden on any one group to adapt to the others.

He hears: she likes it and wants more detail. He spends two days developing it. Then there's awkwardness on both sides. Nobody was rude. They were just speaking different cultural languages, in the same English. In this lecture, you'll learn how culture shapes communication, useful dimensions to understand differences, practical habits for multicultural teams, language and fairness, and how to build cultural intelligence.

And a sensible driver doesn't assume that every driver in a country behaves identically either. Cross-cultural skill is like driving abroad well: notice the conventions, adapt carefully, and watch the actual car in front of you.

Machine translation and live captions can help, but check anything important with a fluent colleague, and never rely on them for contracts, HR matters or safety instructions.

lessons.title: Leading people through change
lessons.body:
### Change is emotional

Organisations change constantly: restructures, new systems, mergers, new strategies, and now AI adoption. Most change initiatives struggle not because the plan is wrong but because people do not adopt the change. Leading change means helping people through the transition, not just announcing the new state.

### Models that help

- **Kotter's eight steps** (a widely used model): create urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a vision, communicate it, empower action by removing obstacles, generate short-term wins, sustain acceleration, and anchor the change in culture.
- **ADKAR** (Prosci): individuals need **A**wareness of the need, **D**esire to participate, **K**nowledge of how to change, **A**bility to implement, and **R**einforcement to sustain it. It is useful for diagnosing where a person or group is stuck.
- **Bridges' transition model:** change is situational (the new system), transition is psychological. People go through **endings** (letting go), a **neutral zone** (uncertainty) and **new beginnings**.

### Diagnosing with ADKAR

| Symptom | Likely gap | Leader action |
|---|---|---|
| "Why are we doing this?" | Awareness | Explain the reasons, with evidence and consequences of not changing |
| "What's in it for me?" / resistance | Desire | Involve people; address concerns; show benefits; leaders role-model |
| "I don't know how." | Knowledge | Training, guides, examples |
| "I tried but can't do it yet." | Ability | Practice, coaching, time, support |
| Slipping back to old ways | Reinforcement | Recognition, measures, removing old options |

### Communicating change

- **Explain why before what and how.**
- **Be honest** about what is known and unknown; uncertainty handled honestly builds trust.
- **Repeat** the message through multiple channels; people need to hear important messages several times.
- **Two-way:** create forums for questions and concerns; answer them visibly.
- **Line managers are key:** people prefer to hear about changes affecting them from their direct manager. Equip managers with briefings and FAQs.

### Change communication template

```
What is changing: ______
Why: ______ (business reason, evidence)
What it means for you: ______ (role, process, tools)
What is not changing: ______
Timeline: ______
Support available: training, help desk, champions
Where to ask questions: ______
What we need from you: ______
```

### Supporting people through transition

- Acknowledge losses (familiar tools, relationships, status) rather than dismissing them.
- Provide stability where possible during the neutral zone.
- Celebrate early wins to build momentum.
- Identify and support **change champions** within teams.
- Watch wellbeing, especially during restructures.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* A fictional insurance company in Dubai introduced AI-assisted claims processing. Claims handlers feared job losses and resisted. Leaders explained the reasons (faster claims, more time for complex cases), were honest that roles would change, and committed to retraining rather than redundancies for the current team. Handlers were involved in testing, and champions in each team shared tips. The company tracked adoption and recognised teams that helped others. Resistance fell as people saw that the tool removed repetitive work and they gained new skills in complex case handling.

### Leading your own response to change

Leaders are also affected by change. Acknowledge your own reactions, seek support and information, and remember that your team watches how you respond. Visible, consistent commitment from leaders is one of the strongest predictors of change adoption.

### Hands-on: an ADKAR diagnostic and a change communication plan

**1. ADKAR diagnostic** (score each group 1–5; the first low score is where to focus):

| Group | Awareness (why) | Desire (want to) | Knowledge (how) | Ability (can do) | Reinforcement (sticks) | First gap → action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Store managers | 4 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 1 | Desire → involve them in pilot design; show time saved |
| Finance team | 5 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 1 | Knowledge → hands-on training + job aids |

**2. Change communication plan:**

```text
Change:            (one sentence, plain words)
Why now:           (the honest reason; what happens if we don't change)
What changes / what stays the same:
Who is affected and how (by group):
What we know / what we don't know yet / when we'll know:
What support is available (training, time, help desk, champions):
How people can ask questions or raise concerns:
Timeline and next update date:
Messengers:        senior sponsor (why) + direct managers (what it means for you)
Channels:          team meetings first, then written FAQ, then recorded briefing
```

**3. An FAQ that you keep updating.** Collect real questions (anonymous form) and answer them weekly. Mark answers as "confirmed" or "not decided yet".

**4. Adoption measures:** usage of the new process/tool, error rates, time to complete, support tickets, and a short pulse question: "I understand why this change is happening and what it means for me" (1–5).

**AI-era note:** when the change involves AI tools, add to the plan what the tool will and won't be used for, what data it can access, how quality is checked, and what happens to roles. Silence on these points fuels rumours.

### Common mistakes

- Announcing the change without explaining why.
- One communication, then silence.
- Ignoring emotions and losses.
- Bypassing line managers.
- Declaring victory too early before new behaviours are embedded.

### Quick self-check

For a change you are leading, estimate where your team is on ADKAR. Which element is weakest, and what one action will you take this week to strengthen it?

### Measuring adoption

Track whether change is actually happening: usage of new systems, completion of training, process compliance, and outcomes such as cycle times or customer satisfaction. Share progress openly and use the data to target support where adoption lags, rather than to blame teams.

### Change fatigue

When organisations run many changes at once, people become exhausted and cynical. Leaders can help by sequencing changes where possible, explaining how initiatives connect, stopping lower-value initiatives, and acknowledging the effort people are making. Ask your team what is consuming their energy; sometimes the most helpful leadership act is removing something rather than adding another initiative.

scenes.narration: Think about the last big change at work: a new system, a restructure, a new way of working, perhaps AI tools arriving in your team. How did people react? Some were enthusiastic. Some were anxious. Some said nothing and quietly carried on the old way. That's normal. Change isn't just a project plan; it's an emotional experience for the people living through it. In this lecture, you'll learn models that help you understand change, how to diagnose where people are stuck with ADKAR, how to communicate change, support people through transition, and measure adoption.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because many change initiatives fail to deliver what they promised, and the reason is rarely the technology or the plan. It's that people don't adopt the change, or adopt it half-heartedly. A new system nobody uses properly is just an expensive system. Leaders who manage the human side of change get faster adoption, less disruption and keep people's trust for the next change. And there's always a next change.

scenes.narration: Here's the concept. Three models help. John Kotter's eight steps focus on leading organisational change: urgency, a guiding coalition, a vision, communication, removing obstacles, quick wins, building on change and anchoring it in culture. William Bridges' transition model says that change is the external event, but transition is the internal, psychological process: an ending, a neutral zone of confusion, then a new beginning. And Prosci's ADKAR model describes what each individual needs: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. Here's the key idea: organisations don't change; people do, one at a time.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of moving house. The move itself happens on one day: that's the change. But the transition takes months. There's the ending: leaving a home full of memories, even if the new one is better. Then the neutral zone: boxes everywhere, you can't find the kettle, your commute is unfamiliar. Then the new beginning: the new place finally feels like home. A good leader in change is like a good friend when you move house. They acknowledge the loss, help you through the boxes, and celebrate when you're settled.

scenes.narration: Now ADKAR as a diagnostic. For each group affected, ask five questions in order. Awareness: do they understand why the change is happening? Desire: do they want to take part? Knowledge: do they know how to change? Ability: can they actually do it in their daily work? And reinforcement: is there anything making it stick? Score each from one to five. The first low score is where to focus, because the later stages don't work without the earlier ones. Training people who don't see why is wasted effort.

• Desire: want to?
• Knowledge: how?
• Ability: can do?
• Reinforcement: sticks?
• Fix the first low score

scenes.narration: Communicating change well is most of the work. Explain why, honestly, including what happens if you don't change. Say what changes and, just as important, what stays the same. Be honest about what you don't know yet, and when you'll know. Use two messengers: a senior sponsor to explain why, and people's direct manager to explain what it means for them, because people usually trust their own manager most. Communicate more than feels necessary, in several channels, and create ways for people to ask questions, including anonymously.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. A small accounting practice in Leeds is moving from spreadsheets to cloud accounting software. The partner, Helen, notices that the two most experienced bookkeepers keep using the old spreadsheets. She runs an ADKAR check. Awareness is fine; they know why. Desire is low: they're worried about looking slow in front of younger colleagues. So Helen asks them to co-design the new workflow and gives them extra practice time before go-live. They become the internal experts.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. A retail bank in Karachi is introducing an AI assistant to help branch staff answer customer questions. Rumours spread that it will replace jobs. The regional head, Ayesha, runs an ADKAR survey. Awareness is patchy and desire is low. She holds branch meetings where she explains why, what the tool will and won't do, how answers are checked, and that no roles are being cut in this phase. She trains branch champions, collects questions weekly, and publishes an updated FAQ. Adoption rises steadily over three months, and complaint handling times fall.

scenes.narration: Supporting people through transition means recognising the neutral zone. Productivity often dips temporarily. People feel uncertain and may grieve what they're losing, even if the change is good. So acknowledge the losses openly. Give extra time and help during the learning period. Create quick wins and share them. Use champions, respected peers who adopt early and help others. And look after yourself too. Leaders go through their own transition, often earlier than their team, and your team will notice your stress. Watch for change fatigue when too many changes arrive at once.

The why: fewer missed deadlines. What stays the same: our weekly review. What we don't know yet: the date old data will be archived. I'll confirm by the end of the month. scenes.narration: How do you measure adoption? Track usage of the new process or tool, error rates, time to complete key tasks, and support tickets. Watch for workarounds, like people keeping the old spreadsheet on the side. Run a short pulse question, such as: I understand why this change is happening and what it means for me. And check reinforcement after three and six months. Many changes succeed at launch and then slowly slide back. Celebrate progress and fix what's making the old way easier.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Announcing change only once, by email. Explaining what without why. Over-promising and hiding what you don't know. Training people before they want to change. Ignoring the emotional side and the losses. Declaring victory at launch. Too many changes at once. And introducing AI tools without explaining what they'll do, what data they use, and what it means for people's roles. Silence fills with rumours.

modules.title: Leading in the AI era: agents, async and responsible AI
modules.summary: Lead teams that work alongside AI agents, run async communication across time zones, and use AI in everyday management without compromising fairness, privacy or trust.

lessons.title: Leading teams that work with AI agents
lessons.body:
### From tools to teammates-with-limits

Most teams now use AI assistants to draft, summarise and analyse. A growing number also use **AI agents**: systems that take a goal, plan steps and act through tools, such as searching a knowledge base, updating a CRM record, drafting and sending an email, triaging support tickets or running a data pipeline. Agents are built into mainstream products (for example assistants in Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and customer-service platforms) and can be built with automation tools such as n8n, Zapier or vendor agent frameworks.

For a leader, the technology details matter less than a management question: **what work do we hand to agents, with how much autonomy, and who is accountable when they get it wrong?** You already know the answer's shape from the delegation lesson.

### Delegating to agents: autonomy levels

Treat an agent like a new, very fast, very literal team member who never gets tired and sometimes confidently makes things up. Match autonomy to risk.

| Level | Agent does | Human does | Suitable for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Assist | Drafts, suggests, summarises | Decides and acts | Client emails, proposals, analysis |
| 2. Recommend | Proposes an action with reasons | Approves each action | Refunds, CRM updates, ticket routing |
| 3. Act with review | Acts; humans sample outputs | Reviews a sample daily/weekly; can undo | Internal tagging, meeting notes, data clean-up |
| 4. Act within limits | Acts inside hard limits (value, scope, recipients) | Monitors metrics and exceptions | Low-value, reversible, high-volume tasks |

Rules of thumb: anything **irreversible, customer-facing, legally significant or about people's jobs, pay or access** stays at level 1 or 2. Start low and move up only with evidence.

### Five leadership responsibilities

1. **A named human owner for every agent workflow.** The owner defines the task, checks quality, fixes problems and answers for results. "The AI did it" is never an acceptable explanation to a client or regulator.
2. **Clear boundaries.** What data can the agent access? What systems can it change? What can it never do? Apply least-privilege access, the same way you would for a new starter.
3. **Quality measurement.** Define what "good" looks like and sample outputs. Track error rate, escalation rate, rework time and customer complaints, not just volume.
4. **Psychological safety to report AI errors.** People must feel safe saying "the agent got this wrong" or "I don't trust this output", without being seen as anti-innovation. Research by Amy Edmondson on psychological safety shows why teams that can speak up learn faster.
5. **Skills and roles.** As agents take routine steps, roles shift towards judgement, exceptions, relationships and supervision. Plan training and talk honestly about what changes.

### Governance and regulation (keep it proportionate)

- In the EU, the AI Act's **AI literacy** obligation (Article 4) has applied since 2 February 2025: providers and deployers must take measures to ensure staff dealing with AI systems have sufficient AI literacy. If your organisation uses AI in the EU, team training is not optional.
- Frameworks such as the **NIST AI Risk Management Framework** (US) and **ISO/IEC 42001** (AI management systems) offer structured approaches for larger organisations.
- Data protection law (for example UK GDPR and EU GDPR, and national laws elsewhere) applies whenever agents process personal data. Involve your data protection lead before connecting agents to customer or employee data.

Check your organisation's AI policy first; this lesson gives general guidance, not legal advice.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Sana leads a six-person customer support team for an e-commerce brand in Lahore. The company introduces an agent that drafts replies and routes tickets. Sana sets it at level 2 for refunds (the agent recommends, a person approves) and level 3 for routing (the agent acts; a team member reviews 20 routed tickets a day). She names Omar as the agent owner, creates a shared "AI error log" and praises the first person who logs a mistake. After a month, routing accuracy is good enough to move to level 4 with limits; refunds stay at level 2 because they involve money and customer trust.

### Hands-on: write an agent charter

Use this one-page charter for every agent workflow your team runs. Review it monthly.

```text
AGENT CHARTER — [workflow name] — v1 [date]
Purpose:            what task, for whom, what outcome
Human owner:        name, role (accountable for results)
Autonomy level:     1 Assist | 2 Recommend | 3 Act with review | 4 Act within limits
Allowed actions:    (e.g. read tickets, draft replies, set tags)
Never allowed:      (e.g. issue refunds, delete records, email external parties without approval)
Data access:        systems + fields; personal data? (DPO consulted: yes/no)
Hard limits:        (value caps, recipients, volume per hour)
Quality checks:     sample size + frequency; what counts as an error
Metrics:            accuracy, escalation rate, rework minutes, complaints
Escalation:         how staff flag problems; how to pause the agent (who can, how fast)
Disclosure:         do customers need to be told they're interacting with AI?
Review date:        monthly; criteria to move autonomy up or down
```

Add a simple RACI line for the workflow so everyone knows who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. The agent can be Responsible for a step; only a person can be Accountable.

### Measuring success

Compare before and after on time saved, quality (errors and rework), customer outcomes and team experience. If time saved comes with rising complaints or hidden rework, the workflow is not working yet.

### Common mistakes

- Giving an agent more autonomy than a new starter would get.
- No named owner, so errors fall between teams.
- Measuring volume processed instead of quality.
- Punishing people who report AI mistakes, which drives errors underground.
- Connecting agents to personal or client data without a data protection review.
- Staying silent about how roles will change, which fuels rumours and resistance.

### Quick self-check

List every AI assistant or agent your team uses. For each, can you name the human owner, its autonomy level and the one metric that shows whether it is working? Any blanks are your first actions.

scenes.narration: Imagine this. It's Monday morning and your customer support team has a new colleague. It works twenty-four hours a day, handles hundreds of tickets, never gets tired, and occasionally, with total confidence, tells a customer something completely wrong. That colleague is an AI agent. More and more teams are working alongside them. The question for you as a leader isn't whether the technology is impressive. It's this: what work do we give it, with how much freedom, and who's accountable when it gets it wrong? In this lecture, you'll learn autonomy levels for agents, five leadership responsibilities, the governance basics, and how to write an agent charter.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter now? Because agents are moving from demos into everyday work. They're built into mainstream office suites and customer-service platforms, and teams can build their own with automation tools. An assistant only suggests. An agent acts: it updates records, routes tickets, sends messages, runs a process. That's powerful, and it changes the leader's job. When an agent makes a mistake, it can repeat it hundreds of times before anyone notices. The management skills you already have, delegation, quality control and building trust, are exactly what make agents safe and useful.

scenes.narration: Here's the concept. Delegate to an agent the way you'd delegate to a new starter, with levels of autonomy. Level one, assist: the agent drafts or summarises, and a person decides and acts. Level two, recommend: the agent proposes an action with reasons, and a person approves each one. Level three, act with review: the agent acts, and people sample the results and can undo them. Level four, act within limits: the agent acts inside hard limits, such as a value cap, and people watch the metrics. Here's the key idea. Anything irreversible, customer-facing, legally significant, or about people's jobs and pay, stays at level one or two.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a hospital bringing in a brilliant new junior doctor. On day one, they don't operate alone. They take histories and suggest diagnoses, and a senior doctor signs off. As they show good judgement, they're trusted with more, but some decisions always need a consultant, and every patient has a named responsible clinician. Agents are like that junior doctor, but faster, more literal, and without the instinct to ask when something feels off. So you need the sign-offs, the named owner and the gradual trust even more.

scenes.narration: Let's dwell on psychological safety, because it's where many teams quietly fail. Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety describes teams where people feel able to speak up about mistakes and concerns without fear. With AI, there's an extra pressure: nobody wants to look like the person who's against innovation. So when the agent routes a ticket wrongly, people quietly fix it and move on. The error never gets logged and the agent never improves. Make reporting easy with a shared AI error log, and publicly thank the first person who uses it.

knowledgeCheck.question: A new agent can issue customer refunds automatically. What is the most appropriate starting autonomy level?
options: Act within limits, with no review

knowledgeCheck.question: Which statement about accountability for an agent workflow is correct?
options: The vendor is accountable for all outcomes
The agent can be accountable if it is well configured
A named human owner is accountable; the agent can only be responsible for steps

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Accountability always sits with a person. 'The AI did it' is not acceptable to clients or regulators.

lessons.title: Async communication that works
lessons.body:
### Why async is a leadership skill

Asynchronous (async) communication means people contribute at different times: written proposals, comments on documents, recorded video walkthroughs, threaded chat and status updates. Synchronous (sync) communication happens in real time: meetings, calls and live chat.

Async is not "fewer meetings" as a slogan. It is a way of working that lets teams across time zones, shift patterns and caring responsibilities contribute fully, protects focus time and creates a written record of decisions. Some fully remote companies (GitLab is a well-known example with a public handbook) document an async-first approach in detail. You do not need to be fully remote to benefit: hybrid and office teams waste the same hours on status meetings and interruptions.

### When to use async and when to meet

| Use async for | Use sync (meet) for |
|---|---|
| Status updates and progress reports | Building relationships, especially with new people |
| Proposals that need thoughtful input | Conflict, sensitive or emotional topics |
| Reviewing documents, designs, code | Complex problems with many unknowns (after a written pre-read) |
| Decisions with a clear owner and deadline | Crises needing rapid coordination |
| Sharing information and walkthroughs | Celebrations and team rituals |

A useful default: **start async; escalate to a meeting when the thread goes in circles or emotions rise.** A good rule is "three rounds and we talk".

### The five building blocks

1. **A written proposal format with a comment deadline.** Owner, context, recommendation, options, open questions, decision date. Silence by the deadline counts as "no objection" only if the team has agreed that rule.
2. **Clear channel norms and response times.** For example: chat, same working day; documents, comment by the stated deadline; email, two working days; urgent, phone. Put them in the team working agreement.
3. **Threads per topic.** One thread per decision or issue, with a clear title. No decisions buried in direct messages.
4. **Recorded walkthroughs.** A 3–5 minute screen recording (for example with Loom, or the recording feature in Microsoft Teams, Zoom or Google Meet, depending on your tools) replaces many "can you walk me through it" meetings. Add a written summary; not everyone can watch video.
5. **A decision log.** Every decision gets a line: what, who decided, when, link to the thread. This is how async teams avoid re-litigating.

### Writing for async

Async only works if messages can be understood without a follow-up call. Apply BLUF (bottom line up front), state exactly what you need from whom by when, include the context a reader in another time zone needs, and link to sources instead of saying "as discussed". Assume the reader has not been in any of your meetings.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* Farah leads an eight-person product team split between Karachi, Dubai and Toronto, with only a two-hour overlap. The daily stand-up was held at a time that suited Dubai, so Toronto joined at dawn and Karachi missed family dinners. She replaced it with an async stand-up in a chat thread by 10:00 local time (yesterday, today, blockers), a weekly 45-minute live meeting in the overlap for problem-solving and connection, and a proposal template with 48-hour comment windows. Blockers were now visible earlier, because they were written down, and the team regained several hours a week.

### Hands-on: three async templates

**1. Async proposal (paste into a shared doc):**

```text
PROPOSAL: [title]              Owner: [name]      Decide by: [date, time + time zone]
Bottom line:   I propose we ___.
Context:       why now; what problem; link to data
Options:       A (recommended) / B / do nothing — pros, cons, cost, risk
Open questions: 1. ___ (I need input from ___)
How to respond: comment in the doc by [deadline]. Say "agree", "agree with changes",
                or "object" with a reason. Silence = no objection (team norm).
Decision rule: owner decides after comments / consent / escalate to ___
```

**2. Async stand-up (in a thread, by an agreed local time):**

```text
Yesterday: shipped X; reviewed Y
Today:     Z
Blockers:  waiting on data export from @name (needed by Thu)
FYI:       out Friday afternoon
```

**3. Recorded walkthrough script (for a 3–5 minute video):**

```text
0:00  What this is and what I need from you (decision/feedback) by when
0:30  Context in two sentences
1:00  Walk through the key screen/document (only what matters)
3:00  Options/risks
3:30  Repeat the ask and the deadline; link to the written summary
```

**AI support:** AI assistants in chat and document tools can summarise long threads and draft decision-log entries. Always have the decision owner check the summary before it is recorded, and follow your team's rules on which tools may process internal data.

### Measuring success

Track time in meetings per person, time to decision, the proportion of decisions logged, blocked-work time and, in pulse surveys, whether people in every time zone feel able to contribute.

### Common mistakes

- Replacing meetings with a flood of unstructured messages.
- No deadlines, so proposals drift for weeks.
- Expecting instant replies, which turns async into "sync with extra steps".
- Videos with no written summary or no clear ask.
- Decisions made in DMs and never logged.
- Using async for conflict or sensitive feedback.

### Quick self-check

Look at your last week. Which meeting could have been an async proposal or a recorded walkthrough? Which long thread should have become a 15-minute call?

lessons.title: Using AI in everyday management, responsibly
lessons.body:
### A capable assistant, not a substitute for judgement

AI assistants can save managers hours each week: drafting messages, summarising documents, preparing for one-to-ones, turning notes into action lists, analysing anonymous survey comments and rehearsing difficult conversations. The risk is not that AI is useless; it is that it is fluent. A polished paragraph can hide a wrong fact, a biased assumption or a tone that is not yours, and your team will judge you, not the tool.

This lesson gives you a practical rule set: where AI helps, where to be careful, and where it should not be used without strong safeguards.

### A traffic-light guide for managers

| Green: use freely (with checks) | Amber: use with care and safeguards | Red: do not use AI to decide |
|---|---|---|
| Drafting routine messages and agendas | Summarising meetings (announce it; human checks) | Hiring, promotion, pay, termination decisions |
| Summarising long documents and threads | Analysing anonymous engagement survey comments | Performance ratings or disciplinary outcomes |
| Preparing questions for a 1:1 or coaching | Drafting feedback from your own notes | Monitoring individuals' productivity or emotions |
| Rehearsing a difficult conversation | Writing job descriptions (check for biased language) | Anything involving health, grievances or protected characteristics |
| Structuring a presentation or plan | Translating messages (check with a fluent speaker) | Pasting confidential data into unapproved tools |

"Red" does not mean AI can never be involved in those processes; it means **a person makes the decision, with proper process, and any AI tool used has been approved, assessed and disclosed**. Many organisations have HR, legal and data protection processes for exactly this.

### Why the red zone matters

- **Fairness and bias.** AI systems can reproduce biases present in their training data or in the way a prompt is framed. A ranking of candidates or a summary of "performance issues" can quietly disadvantage groups.
- **Law.** Data protection law restricts certain solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on people (for example Article 22 of the UK GDPR and EU GDPR). The EU AI Act lists AI used for recruitment, promotion, termination, task allocation and monitoring or evaluating workers as **high-risk**, with obligations that are being phased in (their application date was postponed by 2026 amendments; check the current timetable). Other countries have their own rules; check locally.
- **Trust.** People accept tough decisions more readily when they believe a fair human process was followed. Discovering that a machine wrote your appraisal destroys that belief.

### Transparency with your team

Tell your team how you use AI in management: for example, "I use our approved assistant to draft agendas and summarise documents; I don't use it to evaluate your performance." Agree team norms (see the team working agreement) and follow your organisation's AI policy. When AI has materially shaped something people rely on, such as a summary of their survey comments, say so.

### Protecting data

Use only tools approved by your organisation for the data involved. Do not paste personal data about team members (health, family circumstances, performance concerns, grievances) into consumer tools. Anonymise where you can: roles, not names. Check whether your tool's settings allow inputs to be used for training, and follow your organisation's guidance.

### Worked example

*Illustrative.* James manages a ten-person finance team in Manchester. Before year-end reviews he uses the company's approved assistant to turn his own dated notes (kept throughout the year) into a first-draft structure for each review: achievements, development areas, examples. He then checks every example against his notes, removes a sentence the tool invented about "communication issues", adds context only he knows, and rewrites the opening in his own voice. The rating is decided by him and calibrated with other managers, with no AI involvement. Preparation time falls, and the reviews are more specific than last year's.

### Hands-on: a personal AI use policy and a safe drafting workflow

**1. Write your personal AI use statement** (share it with your team):

```text
How I use AI as a manager
- I use [approved tool] to: draft agendas and routine messages; summarise long documents;
  prepare coaching questions; rehearse difficult conversations.
- I check every fact and rewrite in my own voice before sending.
- I do NOT use AI to: rate performance, decide pay, promotions or discipline,
  or monitor individuals.
- I never paste personal, health or grievance information into AI tools.
- If you're unsure how AI was used in something that affects you, ask me.
```

**2. Safe drafting workflow for feedback or review text:**

```text
Step 1  Write your own bullet notes first (dated, specific, SBI format).
Step 2  Anonymise: roles not names; remove health/family/grievance details.
Step 3  Prompt (approved tool only):
        "Turn these notes into a clear, balanced draft in plain British English.
         Use only the facts given. Do not add examples, judgements or adjectives
         that aren't in the notes. Flag anything that sounds vague or harsh."
Step 4  Check every sentence against your notes; delete anything added.
Step 5  Rewrite the opening and closing in your own words.
Step 6  Deliver in a conversation, not as a pasted document.
```

**3. Survey comment analysis (amber):** remove names and identifying details first; ask for themes with counts and representative (paraphrased) quotes; then read a random sample of raw comments yourself to check the themes are real.

### Measuring success

Time saved on preparation; fewer revisions to your messages; team trust (ask in a pulse survey whether people feel AI is used fairly); and zero data incidents.

### Common mistakes

- Sending AI drafts without checking facts and tone.
- Letting AI "fill gaps" in performance evidence.
- Using consumer tools for personal or confidential information.
- Hidden use that people later discover.
- Treating an AI ranking or summary as objective.

### Quick self-check

Look at the last five things you used AI for at work. Which colour zone was each in? Did you apply the right safeguards?

scenes.narration: Here's a scene that's playing out in offices everywhere. A manager, short of time, asks an AI assistant to write a team member's annual review. It produces three beautifully written paragraphs in seconds. One of them mentions communication issues that never happened. The manager doesn't notice. The team member does. And from that moment, nothing that manager says about performance is fully trusted. AI can save managers hours every week. But its fluency is exactly what makes it risky. In this lecture you'll learn a traffic-light guide for AI in management, why the red zone matters, how to be transparent, how to protect data, and a safe drafting workflow.

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think of a satnav and a driving licence. The satnav is brilliant. It plans routes, spots traffic and saves you time. But if it tells you to turn into a pedestrian street, you don't do it, and if you do, it's your licence, not the satnav's, on the line. AI is your management satnav. Follow it gladly on the motorway of routine drafting. Question it in unfamiliar streets. And never let it drive through the red lights of people decisions. The responsibility always stays with the person holding the licence.

scenes.visual: Layout: a statement card 'How I use AI as a manager' appears pinned in a team channel. 0:20 a padlock icon closes over a folder of personal data; 0:35 a name 'Ayesha K.' morphs into 'Senior analyst' in a prompt box.

scenes.narration: A simple worked example. Asad runs a small accounting firm in Islamabad with seven staff. He uses an approved assistant each Monday to turn his rough notes into a clear weekly plan and an agenda for the team meeting: green zone. When he wants to understand a staff survey, amber zone, he removes names and identifying details first, asks for themes with counts, then reads a random sample of raw comments himself. One theme the tool called workload stress turns out, in the actual comments, to be mostly about unclear priorities. He fixes priorities, not hours.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 1: Asad in Islamabad (illustrative)
• Green: weekly plan and agenda
• Amber: survey themes, anonymised
• Check raw comments
• 'Workload' was really 'unclear priorities'
scenes.visual: Layout: two lanes, green and amber. 0:00 the green lane shows notes turning into an agenda; 0:15 the amber lane shows a survey file passing through an 'anonymise' filter; 0:30 a theme chart appears; 0:40 a magnifying glass on raw comments relabels one bar from 'workload' to 'unclear priorities'.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, illustrative. James manages a ten-person finance team in Manchester. Before year-end reviews, he uses the company's approved assistant to turn his own dated notes, kept throughout the year, into a first-draft structure for each review. He instructs it to use only the facts given. Then he checks every sentence against his notes. In one draft, he finds a sentence about communication issues that isn't in his notes at all. He deletes it. He rewrites openings in his own voice. The ratings are his, calibrated with other managers, with no AI involvement. Preparation time falls, and the reviews are more specific than last year's.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 2: James in Manchester (illustrative)
• Own dated notes first
• 'Use only the facts given'
• Invented sentence found and deleted
• Own voice
• Ratings: human, calibrated
scenes.visual: Layout: a notes document on the left and a draft review on the right. 0:00 lines connect note entries to draft sentences; 0:20 one draft sentence has no connecting line and flashes red; 0:30 it is deleted; 0:45 a rating dial set by a person icon, with a calibration table beside it and no AI icon.

scenes.narration: Let's make the safe drafting workflow explicit, because it applies to feedback, reviews and any sensitive message. Step one, write your own notes first: dated, specific, in situation, behaviour, impact form. Step two, anonymise. Step three, use an approved tool and tell it to use only the facts given, not to add examples, judgements or adjectives, and to flag anything vague or harsh. Step four, check every sentence against your notes and delete additions. Step five, rewrite the opening and closing in your own words. Step six, deliver it in a conversation, not as a pasted document.
scenes.onScreen:
Safe drafting workflow
1 Your notes first
2 Anonymise
3 'Use only these facts'
4 Check every sentence
5 Your own voice
6 Deliver in person
scenes.visual: Layout: a six-step horizontal pipeline, each step lighting in sequence every nine seconds with an icon: notebook, mask, lock-and-prompt, magnifying glass, pen, two chairs. 0:55 a banner 'your evidence stays the source of truth'.

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I write my personal AI use statement for an illustrative team. I use our approved assistant to draft agendas and routine messages, summarise long documents, prepare coaching questions and rehearse difficult conversations. I check every fact and rewrite in my own voice. I don't use AI to rate performance, decide pay, promotions or discipline, or to monitor individuals. I never paste personal, health or grievance information into AI tools. If you're unsure, ask me. Then I classify my last five uses. Four are green. One, summarising a team retrospective, is amber, and I realise I didn't tell the team. I'll mention it at the next meeting.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me: AI use statement + audit
• What I use it for
• What I don't
• Data rule
• 'Ask me'
• Audit: 4 green, 1 amber
• Fix: tell the team
scenes.visual: Layout: screen-recording style document titled 'How I use AI as a manager'. 0:00 bullet lines type in; 0:30 a separate five-row table appears with coloured dots; 0:45 four rows turn green and one amber; 0:55 a note 'tell the team at Monday's meeting' is added.

scenes.narration: How do you know you're using AI well? Measure time saved on preparation. Look at how often you have to correct or retract something you sent. Ask in a pulse survey whether people feel AI is used fairly and transparently in the team. And aim for zero data incidents: nothing personal or confidential pasted into tools that shouldn't have it. If time saved is high but trust is falling, slow down. Trust is the harder thing to rebuild.
scenes.onScreen:
Measuring success
• Preparation time saved
• Fewer corrections
• Pulse: 'AI is used fairly here'
• Zero data incidents
• Trust over speed
scenes.visual: Layout: four KPI tiles. 0:00 'time saved' rises; 0:10 'corrections' falls; 0:20 a pulse-survey score gauge; 0:30 a 'data incidents: 0' counter; 0:40 a scale tipping towards 'trust' over 'speed'.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Sending AI drafts without checking facts and tone. Letting AI fill gaps in performance evidence with plausible sentences. Using consumer tools for personal or confidential information. Using AI secretly, and being found out. Treating an AI ranking or summary as objective, when it reflects its data and your prompt. Using AI to monitor individuals' activity or mood. And outsourcing empathy: an AI-written apology or thank-you that you don't personally mean.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Unchecked drafts
• AI-filled evidence gaps
• Consumer tools for personal data
• Secret use
• 'Objective' AI rankings
• Monitoring individuals
• Outsourced empathy

scenes.narration: Let's recap. AI can save managers hours, but its fluency hides errors, bias and the wrong tone. Use the traffic-light guide: green with checks, amber with safeguards, and red for people decisions that humans must make through proper process. Be transparent, protect data, and use the six-step safe drafting workflow. Your try this now: write your personal AI use statement using the template in the lesson, share it with your team, and classify your last five uses of AI by colour. That completes this course. Well done. Now pick one template from each module and use it this month.

keyTakeaways: AI saves managers time on drafting, summarising and preparation, but fluency can hide errors, bias and the wrong tone.
Use a traffic-light rule: green for routine drafting, amber with safeguards, red where people decisions must be made by humans.
Employment decisions carry legal, fairness and trust risks; data protection and AI laws apply.
Be transparent with your team about how you use AI, and never paste personal or grievance data into unapproved tools.
Write your own notes first, constrain the tool to your facts, check every sentence, and deliver feedback in person.

knowledgeCheck.question: A manager asks an AI tool to rank team members for promotion based on their chat activity. What is the main problem?
options: Promotion is a people decision with fairness and legal implications; it must be made by a person through a proper process, not by an AI ranking
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Employment decisions are in the red zone: bias, law and trust all require human decisions with proper process.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is the safest way to use AI when drafting annual review text?
options: Ask the AI to write the review from the employee's name and role
Write dated notes first, anonymise, instruct the tool to use only those facts, then check every sentence
Paste the full HR file into a consumer chatbot
Let the AI suggest the rating
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Your own evidence stays the source of truth; the tool only structures it, and you remove anything it adds.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why tell your team how you use AI as a manager?
options: It is required in every country
Transparency protects trust; people accept decisions more readily when they know how they were made
It makes the AI more accurate
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Hidden use that is later discovered damages trust; a short, clear statement prevents that.

lessons.activity: Write and share your personal 'How I use AI as a manager' statement, then classify the last five things you used AI for as green, amber or red.

pool.question: An experienced, motivated engineer is given a task she has done many times. Which leadership style fits best?
options: Directing: detailed instructions and close supervision
Delegating: agree the outcome and step back
Coaching: frequent explanation of each step
pool.explanation: High competence and commitment call for delegation; directing would feel like micromanagement.

pool.question: A new manager delegates a report but checks every paragraph daily and rewrites parts. What is the main problem?
options: Micromanaging after delegating undermines ownership and development
The task was too small to delegate
The report should not have a deadline
pool.explanation: Check-ins should match the agreed level and the person's experience; constant rewriting takes the task back.

pool.question: Which elements belong in a good delegation conversation? (Select all that apply.)
options: Why the task matters and what 'done' looks like
The level of authority being given
An instruction not to ask any questions
pool.explanation: Context, authority level and check-ins equip people to succeed; discouraging questions sets them up to fail.

pool.question: In the GROW coaching model, what does the 'O' stand for?
pool.explanation: GROW is Goal, Reality, Options, Will (Way forward).

pool.question: A high performer has become disengaged. In a one-to-one she says she has been doing the same work for two years and sees no path to grow. Which response best addresses the underlying need?
options: Co-create a development plan with a stretch assignment and mentoring, and review it regularly
Tell her to be grateful for stable work
Reduce her workload without discussing growth
Give a one-off bonus and move on
pool.explanation: Her need is mastery and growth; money or reduced workload does not address it.

pool.question: Which statement about trust is most accurate?
options: It grows from competence, reliability and care, and can be lost quickly
It cannot be rebuilt once lost
It comes automatically with a job title
It is built mainly by being liked
pool.explanation: Trust is earned through consistent behaviour; titles and popularity are not substitutes.

pool.question: Why are one-to-ones valuable?
options: They give regular space for support, feedback and development, led by the team member's topics
They are mainly for the manager's status updates
They are only needed during performance problems
pool.explanation: Regular one-to-ones build trust and catch issues early.

pool.question: Which piece of feedback is most useful?
options: In yesterday's client call, you summarised the three risks clearly, and the client agreed to our plan
pool.explanation: Specific behaviour and impact tell the person what to repeat.

pool.question: Your colleague repeatedly misses handoff deadlines. What is the best first step?
options: A private SBI conversation that asks for their perspective
Report them to senior management immediately
Mention it publicly in the team meeting
pool.explanation: Timely, private, specific feedback with curiosity is most likely to resolve the issue.

pool.question: Two managers argue over a shared budget. One wants it for marketing to hit growth targets; the other for system upgrades to reduce outages. What approach is most likely to produce a good outcome?
options: Split the budget exactly in half
Explore both interests and look for options such as phasing or targeting spend where it serves both
Let the more senior manager win
pool.explanation: Interest-based problem-solving can find options that satisfy both needs; splitting or deferring may serve neither.

pool.question: Which are part of preparing for a difficult conversation? (Select all that apply.)
options: Separating observed facts from your assumptions
Considering the other person's likely perspective
Deciding in advance that they are wrong
pool.explanation: Preparation builds clarity and empathy; prejudging closes down dialogue.

pool.question: Someone gives you blunt, critical feedback. What is the most constructive first response?
options: Listen, ask for a specific example and thank them
pool.explanation: Listening and clarifying helps you extract value from feedback even if delivery is poor.

pool.question: When is the 'accommodating' conflict style most appropriate?
options: When a quick unpopular decision is needed
When the issue matters much more to the other person than to you, or you realise you are wrong
pool.explanation: Accommodating preserves relationships on low-stakes issues; overuse creates resentment.

pool.question: During mediation between two team members, each keeps restating their position. What technique helps most?
options: Ask each to paraphrase the other's view until the other agrees it is accurate
pool.explanation: Accurate paraphrasing builds understanding and shifts the discussion toward interests.

pool.question: Which email opening follows BLUF?
options: There are several things to consider
As you may recall from our meeting last month
I hope you are well; I wanted to give some background
Please approve the revised launch date of 12 May by Thursday; details below
pool.explanation: BLUF puts the request and deadline first; the other openings delay the point and risk the reader missing it.

pool.question: A weekly two-hour meeting has 15 attendees and mostly status updates. Which changes would help? (Select all that apply.)
options: Add more slides to each update
Reduce attendees to those needed for decisions
Move status updates to a written summary
Shorten the meeting and add a pre-read
pool.explanation: Written updates, fewer attendees and pre-reads cut waste; more slides adds to it.

pool.question: In a decision meeting, the CEO states her preferred option first and everyone agrees. What bias is most likely at play?
pool.explanation: When a senior leader speaks first, others tend to defer and anchor on that view.

pool.question: What should meeting notes include?
options: Decisions, actions with owners and deadlines, and parked items
pool.explanation: Concise notes focused on decisions and actions drive follow-through.

pool.question: A team must decide whether to try a new stand-up format (easy to reverse) and whether to sign a 5-year office lease (hard to reverse). How should they allocate effort?
options: Try the stand-up format quickly and learn; invest more analysis and consultation in the lease
pool.explanation: Reversible decisions favour speed and experimentation; irreversible ones justify deeper analysis.

pool.question: Which technique best reduces groupthink in a strategy discussion?
options: Limiting the discussion to five minutes
Assigning someone to argue the strongest case against the preferred option
Asking the most senior person to speak first
pool.explanation: A devil's advocate or red team surfaces risks the group might suppress.

pool.question: In the pyramid principle, what comes first?
pool.explanation: Readers get the answer first, then supporting arguments and evidence.

pool.question: A regulator has high power and moderate interest in your initiative. How should you engage them?
options: Let a junior colleague handle it informally
Keep satisfied: proactive, accurate, focused engagement at key points
pool.explanation: High-power stakeholders can block initiatives; they require careful, proactive engagement.

pool.question: You need IT security's approval for a new tool. Which approach is most likely to succeed?
options: Send a long email with no clear request
Show how the tool reduces their risk of unsanctioned apps, propose a controlled pilot and meet one-to-one first
Start using the tool and ask forgiveness later
pool.explanation: Aligning with their interests and lowering risk with a pilot builds support.

pool.question: Which uses of persuasion principles are unethical? (Select all that apply.)
options: Claiming peer teams adopted a tool when they have not
Sharing genuine results from a pilot
Inventing a deadline to pressure a decision
pool.explanation: Fake scarcity, false social proof and inflated authority are manipulative; sharing real results is ethical.

pool.question: Your manager is anxious and micromanages after a past error. What is the most constructive approach?
options: Offer earlier drafts and a quality checklist to build confidence
pool.explanation: Addressing the manager's underlying anxiety with earlier drafts and a checklist often restores autonomy; refusing, complaining or working around them escalates the problem.

pool.question: What is a key habit of managing up?
options: Wait for your manager to ask
No surprises: raise problems early with options
pool.explanation: Early, solution-focused communication builds trust; hiding bad news, waiting to be asked or public disagreement erode it.

pool.question: Sales managers you rated 'low interest' control data your project depends on, and data quality is poor. What should you do?
options: Re-map them as 'manage closely' and co-design the data process with them
Build the project without their data
pool.explanation: Stakeholder maps must be updated when you learn someone has more influence than assumed.

pool.question: What is the main reason to show stakeholders how their input changed a plan?
options: It demonstrates their input matters, sustaining engagement and trust
It is a legal requirement everywhere
It removes the need for approval
pool.explanation: Showing how input changed the plan proves it mattered and encourages continued participation; it is not mainly about length, approvals or legal rules.

pool.question: Which chart best compares sales across six product categories?
options: A pie chart with six slices
A line chart with random order
pool.explanation: Sorted bars make comparisons across categories easy; many-slice pies, 3D shapes and unordered lines make them harder.

pool.question: Only the headline of each slide is read aloud to a colleague, and the story is unclear. What should you fix first?
options: Rewrite headlines as full-sentence messages that build the story
Add more data to each slide
pool.explanation: Headlines carry the storyline; fix them before design details.

pool.question: Your analysis shows that customers who attend webinars spend more. Which statement is most responsible to present?
options: Webinars cause higher spend, so all customers must attend
Webinar attendance is associated with higher spend; we propose a test to see whether inviting more customers increases spend
pool.explanation: Correlation may reflect motivated customers; proposing a test avoids overstating causation.

pool.question: Which practices make a chart clearer? (Select all that apply.)
options: Label data directly instead of using a legend
Highlight the key series and grey out the rest
pool.explanation: Focus, direct labels and insight headlines aid understanding; 3D and clutter hinder it.

pool.question: An executive asks a question you cannot answer. What should you do?
options: Say you don't know, commit to a follow-up time, and follow up
pool.explanation: Honesty and reliable follow-up protect credibility; inventing answers, ignoring questions or blaming others destroys it.

pool.question: In SCQA, which element states the recommended action?
pool.explanation: The resolution answers the question created by the complication.

pool.question: Your 20-minute slot is cut to 5 minutes as you walk in. What is the best approach?
options: Skip the ask to save time
Speak very fast through all slides
Present the executive summary: recommendation, key reasons and the ask, offering detail if needed
pool.explanation: A strong summary slide lets you secure the decision even with little time.

pool.question: Which practice helps remote team members feel included in decisions?
options: Only inviting office staff to meetings
Documenting decisions in a shared log before they take effect
pool.explanation: Written, shared decisions give remote and office staff equal access; corridor or private decisions exclude people.

pool.question: A team spans London and Lahore. Which working agreement elements are most helpful? (Select all that apply.)
options: A shared calendar of holidays and working weeks
Requiring everyone to work head-office hours
pool.explanation: Overlap windows, response norms and shared calendars respect both locations; forcing one location's hours is unfair.

pool.question: A manager interprets colleagues' silence in meetings as agreement, but problems surface later. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: Meetings are too short; make them longer
The colleagues are uninterested; exclude them
Cultural or hierarchical reluctance to disagree openly; use specific questions and private or written input
pool.explanation: In many contexts silence does not mean agreement; alternative channels surface concerns.

pool.question: In ADKAR, what does the 'K' represent?
pool.explanation: ADKAR stands for Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement.

pool.question: Staff understand why an AI claims tool is being introduced and have been trained, but many fear job loss and quietly avoid using it. Which ADKAR element needs attention and how?
options: Desire: address concerns honestly, involve staff, clarify role changes and support
Knowledge: run the same training again
pool.explanation: Fear of loss affects desire; honesty, involvement and clear commitments help more than repeating reasons or punishment.

pool.question: Why are line managers important in change communication?
options: They can avoid explaining the reasons
Employees prefer hearing about personal impacts from their direct manager, who can answer questions
pool.explanation: Employees prefer hearing about personal impacts from their direct manager, so equipping line managers improves understanding and trust.

pool.question: Your team adopts an AI agent that can issue customer refunds. Which starting set-up best reflects good leadership practice?
options: Let the agent issue all refunds automatically to save time
The agent recommends each refund and a named person approves it, with a review of autonomy after evidence
pool.explanation: Refunds involve money and trust, so start at 'recommend' with human approval. Autonomy can rise later with evidence; vendors cannot be accountable for your customer decisions.

pool.question: An agent in a Dubai agency emailed one client a report containing another client's data. What should the managing director do first?
options: Blame the analyst who built the agent
Pause the agent, inform and apologise to affected clients, then fix the system (access limits, approval before sending) and record it in an agent charter
Keep the agent running and hope it does not recur
Switch to a different AI vendor immediately without investigating
pool.explanation: Contain, be honest with those affected, then fix the system rather than the blame. Data incidents may also require involving your data protection lead under your organisation's policy.

pool.question: Which elements belong in an agent charter for a team workflow? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A named human owner accountable for results
Actions the agent is never allowed to take
A promise that the agent will never make mistakes
Quality checks with sample size and frequency
A way for staff to pause the agent quickly
pool.explanation: A charter sets ownership, boundaries, quality checks and a pause mechanism. No agent can be promised to be error-free; the charter exists because errors happen.

pool.question: Team members quietly fix an agent's mis-routed tickets without reporting them, because they 'don't want to look negative about AI'. What is the best leadership response?
options: Create a shared AI error log, publicly thank people who report errors and review it in the team meeting
Tell the team the agent is always right
Replace the team with more agents
pool.explanation: This is a psychological safety problem. Making reporting easy and valued surfaces errors so the workflow can improve; hidden fixes let the same error repeat.

pool.question: A proposal thread has gone back and forth three times and people are getting frustrated. According to good async practice, what next?
options: Move to a short call, then write the outcome back into the thread and decision log
Delete the thread and start a new one
pool.explanation: 'Three rounds and we talk': async works until it circles or emotions rise. Recording the outcome afterwards preserves the benefit of a written record.

pool.question: Farah's team spans Karachi, Dubai and Toronto with two hours of overlap. Which change best applies async principles?
options: Hold the daily stand-up at a time convenient for head office
Replace the daily stand-up with a written thread update by 10:00 local time, and keep one weekly live meeting in the overlap
Ask each person to call the manager individually every day
pool.explanation: Written stand-ups let everyone contribute in their own day, while a short live meeting in the overlap keeps connection and handles complex problems.

pool.question: Which features make an async proposal likely to reach a timely decision? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A decide-by date including the time zone
A clear statement of how to respond (agree, agree with changes, object with reason)
A named decision rule or decider
pool.explanation: Deadlines, response options and a decision rule turn comments into decisions. 'As discussed' excludes readers who were not in the conversation.

pool.question: A manager wants to use an AI tool to rank staff for promotion using their chat and email activity. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Proceed if the tool is expensive
Do not let AI decide; promotion is a people decision requiring a fair human process, and such uses raise fairness, data protection and AI-regulation issues that need HR and legal review
pool.explanation: Employment decisions are in the 'red zone'. Activity data is not performance, rankings can embed bias, and laws such as GDPR Article 22 and the EU AI Act's high-risk employment category apply.

pool.question: Which is the safest workflow for using AI to help draft an annual review?
options: Paste the employee's HR file into a consumer chatbot and send its output
Write your own dated notes first, anonymise, instruct an approved tool to use only those facts, check every sentence and deliver the review in a conversation
Ask the AI to suggest the rating
Let the employee's peers write it with AI
pool.explanation: Your evidence remains the source of truth; the tool only structures it. Checking removes invented content, and delivery in person protects trust.

pool.question: When summarising anonymous engagement-survey comments with AI, which step most improves accuracy?
options: Asking the tool for a single overall score
Reading a random sample of the raw comments yourself to check the themes the tool produced
Publishing the AI summary without review
pool.explanation: AI themes can mislabel issues (for example 'workload' when comments are about unclear priorities). Sampling raw comments validates the summary; names should be removed, not added.
